OS1 Kernel Code Guide

Every line of the kernel's h/ and src/, in the order the machine runs it, with the reasons behind it, the questions an examiner is likely to ask, and live-modification drills tested in the sandbox.

32source files (19 in h/, 13 in src/)
2629lines, every non-blank one shown once

How to use this guide

This guide walks through all 32 files of the kernel's h/ and src/. Every line of code is shown exactly once, in the chapter that explains it. Only the blank lines between pieces are left out. The public tests in test/ and the faculty's lib/ are not covered. When the kernel uses something from lib/hw.h, the relevant constants are summarised in chapter 2.

The chapters follow the order the machine runs things: boot, memory, the user side, the trap, the dispatcher, threads, semaphores, the console, and the C++ API on top. After those come end-to-end traces that follow one event through every layer, then a cheat sheet of invariants, a question bank, a file index and a Serbian glossary.

Reading the code blocks

Every listing is copied from your source files when the guide is generated, not typed by hand. The numbers down the left side are the real line numbers in your file. Clicking a number gives you a link to that exact line. A link such as tcb.cpp:108–129 in the prose jumps to the lines it names and highlights the first one.

Most files are shown in several consecutive pieces, each with a short explanation. A few files are split across chapters because their parts belong to different subsystems. For example, asm_routines.cpp holds both the trap entry (chapter 6) and the context switch (chapter 8). The file index in the last chapter lists where every piece of every file is explained.

The boxes

The reasoning behind a design choice: what the alternative was and why it lost. This is what you say when the examiner asks "zašto?".

Something that was measured or checked, in the sandbox on the faculty-equivalent toolchain (GCC 9.4, binutils 2.34, the project's own Makefile with no build tweaks, the faculty's hw.lib), or by reading the assignment PDF. These boxes also say how it was checked.

A reasoned guess that was not checked, such as what an examiner is likely to ask or how the faculty VM differs. Treat these as likely, not certain.

Something that breaks easily when you change the code. Read these before a live modification.

What the assignment text (Projektni zadatak 2026 v1.0) requires, quoted in Serbian where the exact words matter.

Questions and drills

Each chapter ends with likely oral questions and their answers. The answers are hidden until you click, so you can test yourself. The button at the top of the contents opens or closes all answers at once. Chapter 14 collects every question in one list.

Some chapters also include live-modification drills: typical on-the-spot changes, each shown as a patch with the exact files and functions to touch, followed by a small test. Every drill patch was applied to a copy of the project in the sandbox, built with the faculty-equivalent toolchain, and run. The drill says what the run printed.

Practise a drill the way the defence runs it. Read only the task, make the change yourself in CLion on the VM, build, and run the test. Then compare your change with the patch. Undo the change afterwards (git stash, or keep a clean copy of the project), because the submission must stay as it is.

The drills were chosen from modifications that are typical for this course: a new system call, thread_join, sem_trywait, a change of scheduling or allocation policy, time slicing. The examiner may ask for something else. What carries over is the method each drill uses: which layers a change passes through, and which invariant it must not break.

Does this guide match your code?

The guide was generated from sources whose fingerprint is dbb25ba100d17ada69938318154740be. To check your copy, run this in project-base-v1.1 on the VM:

(export LC_ALL=C; md5sum h/* src/* | md5sum)

If it prints the same value, every line number in this guide is exact. If it prints something else, the code has changed since the guide was generated, and line numbers near the changes may be off. export LC_ALL=C inside the parentheses fixes the order in which the shell expands h/* and src/*. In an English locale, trap_frame.hpp would otherwise sort before trap.hpp and the fingerprint would differ although no file has changed. Writing LC_ALL=C md5sum h/* … without export is not enough, because the shell expands the file names before the setting takes effect.

A suggested way through

  1. Read chapter 1 in one sitting. It holds the five decisions that everything else follows from.
  2. Read chapters 2–11 in order, one or two a day, with the code open in CLion alongside.
  3. Read the traces in chapter 12 last. If a trace surprises you, go back to the chapter it links to.
  4. In the days before the defence, work through the question bank with the answers closed, and do every drill once on a copy of the project.

  • The system in one picture
    • <

    Read this chapter before any code. It covers what the program is, how its layers talk to each other, and the five decisions that explain almost every line in the chapters after it.

    What the program is

    The kernel is a library kernel. Your code, hw.lib and the tests are linked into one binary called kernel, which QEMU loads at 0x80000000. There is one physical address space, no paging, and one processor. "Threads" are flows of control inside that single program. There are no processes.

    hw.lib starts the machine in machine mode, sets up the timer and memory protection, drops to supervisor mode and calls main(), our entry point. From there the kernel runs in supervisor mode. Everything above the ABI (the C API, the C++ API, the tests) runs in user mode. The mode is not decided by where the code sits in the binary. Every function is in the same image. The mode is set by the processor's privilege level when the code runs. A thread enters user mode for the first time in exactly one place, threadStart (chapter 8). After that, every return to user mode is the sret at the end of trapEntry, and the only way back up into the kernel is a trap.

    The layers

    The assignment fixes the four layers above the line: the C++ API, the C API, the ABI (the ecall convention) and the trap entry. It also fixes their interfaces (syscall_c.h, syscall_cpp.hpp, the system call codes). The kernel underneath is ours to design.

    Five decisions that shape everything

    1. Kernel code runs on the calling thread's own stack. A system call does not move to a separate kernel stack. trapEntry pushes the user registers onto the stack the thread is already using, then calls C++ functions that push their frames below. So a system call is just a chain of nested calls in that thread's own flow of control. That means a thread can give the processor away in the middle of a system call: thread_dispatch, a sem_wait that blocks, and a getc with no character yet all do. When the thread gets the processor back, it carries on from inside the kernel. The PDF names this the simplest variant. Its advice, which is not binding, is that a separate kernel stack per thread is safer, because a user stack overflow can then not corrupt kernel frames. Running on the thread's own stack was a deliberate choice, and the stack usage was measured (chapter 8).

    2. No interrupt is ever enabled. The kernel is cooperative. A thread loses the processor only when it asks for it (dispatch, blocking wait, exit, waiting for the console) or when it faults. That makes the entire kernel one critical section by construction. Nothing can interrupt kernel code, so no data structure needs a lock. This was the scope decision: zadaci 1–3, without the asynchronous context switch of zadatak 4. Switching interrupts off takes a positive act, which chapter 3 explains.

    3. A thread's context lives on its stack; the control block stores only sp. The picture below shows what a non-running thread's stack holds. Registers are saved twice, in two different places, for two different reasons. The trap frame holds the user-mode registers at the moment of the ecall. The yield frame holds the few registers the kernel's own code needs preserved at the moment of the switch. Chapters 6 and 8 cover each.

    4. The handles are the kernel's own classes. syscall_c.h declares typedef _thread *thread_t and typedef _sem *sem_t. Rather than cast those pointers to some separate internal class, _thread is the thread control block and _sem is the kernel semaphore. The handle a user holds is a pointer to the real kernel object, with no casts and no lookup table. This is also why those two classes are global and not inside namespace kernel.

    5. The kernel never calls its own system calls. Kernel code never uses mem_alloc, the global operator new or ecall. The global new is wired to mem_alloc, which is a system call, so the kernel would trap into itself. Kernel objects come from SlotAllocator storage through a class-specific operator new. The first user thread is created by calling _thread::create directly. Only user code ever executes ecall, so an ecall from supervisor mode is treated as a kernel bug (chapter 6).

    Two smaller choices complete the picture. The ready queue is first come, first served (FCFS). The boot flow of control becomes the main thread, which also serves as the idle thread: it takes a turn in the ready queue like everyone else and halts the machine once no user thread is left.

    Who calls whom

    A system call starts in user code and ends in a kernel object. On the way back it passes through the same layers in reverse order:

    Step Where What happens
    1 C++ API a method such as Semaphore::wait() calls the C API function
    2 C API sem_wait(id) calls __syscall(0x23, id, 0, 0, 0)
    3 ABI __syscall is two instructions: ecall, ret
    4 hardware saves pc in sepc, records the mode in sstatus.SPP, sets scause = 8, jumps to stvec
    5 trap trapEntry saves all 30 registers + sepc + sstatus on the stack, calls trapHandler(frame)
    6 trap trapHandler sees scause == 8, advances frame->sepc by 4, calls Syscalls::dispatch
    7 dispatcher switch (frame.a0) picks the case, reads arguments from frame.a1…a4
    8 kernel object _sem::wait(1) does the work, possibly switching to another thread and coming back later
    9 dispatcher writes the result into frame.a0
    10 trap trapEntry's second half restores every register from the frame and executes sret

    After step 10 the thread is back in user mode, one instruction past its ecall, and a0 holds the result. No other register has changed.

    Questions

    Q1Describe your kernel in two sentences.

    A cooperative library kernel for RV64 in which the kernel runs in supervisor mode on each thread's own stack, and user code runs in user mode above a C API, a C++ API and an ecall-based ABI. Threads switch only when they ask to (dispatch, a blocking semaphore wait, waiting for the console, exit) or when they fault. With no interrupts enabled, the whole kernel is one critical section and needs no locks.

    Q2Is your kernel preemptive?

    No, neither for user code nor inside the kernel. Preempting user code on the timer is zadatak 4, which is out of scope, so no interrupt source is enabled. Chapter 8 has a drill that adds time slicing, to show what that change would take.

    Q3Where does kernel code run: on which stack?

    On the stack of the thread that made the system call. trapEntry pushes the trap frame onto the current sp, and the kernel's C++ frames go below it. There is no separate kernel stack. That is why a system call can switch threads half way through and resume later.

    Q4Why is _thread not in namespace kernel, when every other kernel class is?

    syscall_c.h declares the global name class _thread; typedef _thread *thread_t;, and the assignment fixes that header. A kernel::_thread would be a different class, and the handle would need a cast. Making the global _thread the control block itself removes the cast. _sem is global for the same reason.

    Q5What is the difference between user mode and supervisor mode in this system, given there is no memory protection between them?

    Privilege, not memory. hw.lib configures PMP so user mode can read, write and execute all of memory. What user mode cannot do is execute privileged instructions or access supervisor CSRs (sstatus, sepc, sie and the rest). Public test 7 checks exactly that: csrr t6, sepc in a user thread must raise an illegal instruction fault.

  • Foundations: shared names, error codes, CSRs
    • <

    Three small headers are used almost everywhere: the error codes, the two diagnostic functions borrowed from hw.lib, and the class that wraps the supervisor control registers. First, a look at the faculty header that everything includes.

    What lib/hw.h gives us

    lib/hw.h is the faculty's file, not ours, so it is not listed here. Ten of the nineteen headers include it (#include "../lib/hw.h"), and these are the names from it that the kernel uses:

    Name Value Used for
    uint8 … uint64, size_t, time_t unsigned char … unsigned long every integer type in the kernel; there is no <cstdint>
    DEFAULT_STACK_SIZE 4096 the size of every thread's stack
    MEM_BLOCK_SIZE 64 the allocation unit of mem_alloc and of the ABI
    HEAP_START_ADDR, HEAP_END_ADDR extern const void *, defined in hw.lib the range the memory allocator manages
    CONSOLE_STATUS, CONSOLE_TX_DATA, CONSOLE_RX_DATA extern const uint64, defined in hw.lib UART register addresses
    CONSOLE_TX_STATUS_BIT, CONSOLE_RX_STATUS_BIT 1 << 5, 1 "can send" and "can read" bits of the status register
    DEFAULT_TIME_SLICE, CONSOLE_IRQ, plic_claim, plic_complete   not used: they belong to zadatak 4

    Values read from the kernel image built in the sandbox (GCC 9.4) with nm and objdump: HEAP_START_ADDR = 0x8000d190, which is end, the first address past the kernel's .bss. HEAP_END_ADDR = 0x88000000, the end of QEMU's 128 MiB of RAM. CONSOLE_STATUS = 0x10000005 and CONSOLE_TX_DATA = CONSOLE_RX_DATA = 0x10000000, which are the line status register and the data register of QEMU's 16550 UART. The heap start moves whenever the kernel image grows or shrinks, so your VM build will show a slightly different value.

    Five of these constants are extern: the two heap bounds and the three UART addresses are defined in hw.lib rather than written into the header. So their values are not compile-time constants in our code. This matters in chapter 10: a global initialised from CONSOLE_STATUS would need code to run at start-up, and nothing runs such code in this kernel.

    h/error_codes.hpp: one error vocabulary

    h/error_codes.hpp23 lines · in the submission zip as inc/error_codes.hpp

    The assignment says only that every call returns 0 or a valid value on success and a negative number on failure. The specific codes are ours. They are used in both directions across the ABI: kernel functions return them internally, the dispatcher sends them to user mode through a0, and the C API returns them to the program unchanged. Some come straight from the user side without any trap. thread_create returns SYS_ERR_BAD_ARGUMENT for a null handle before it allocates anything (syscall_c.cpp:36).

    Code Value Where it comes from
    SYS_ERR_GENERIC −1 an unknown system call code; a second Thread::start(); _thread::exit refusing the main thread (a defensive check, unreachable through the C API)
    SYS_ERR_NO_MEMORY −2 no stack for thread_create; no slot for a _thread or _sem
    SYS_ERR_BAD_HANDLE −3 a sem_t that is not an open semaphore
    SYS_ERR_BAD_ARGUMENT −4 a null or unaligned handle pointer, a null body, a stack that is not a live block, a bad mem_free pointer
    SYS_ERR_SEM_CLOSED −5 a sem_wait interrupted because the semaphore was closed
    SYS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED −6 time_sleep, which needs a timer this kernel does not run

    It is a plain enum, not an enum class, so each value converts implicitly to int. The C API functions return int, and the kernel stores results in int fields such as _thread::waitResult. A scoped enum would need a cast at every one of those places.

    h/kdebug.hpp: printing from the kernel

    h/kdebug.hpp15 lines · in the submission zip as inc/kdebug.hpp

    Both functions are defined in hw.lib, which is a stripped-down xv6. __printf is a small printf in the style of xv6's. The kernel uses only %s and %p with it. It writes straight to the UART, bypassing our console layer. The kernel uses it in exactly one place: the fault report in trap.cpp:44–52. panic prints its message and then spins for ever. It never halts the emulator, which matters in chapter 6.

    __attribute__((noreturn)) tells the compiler that control never comes back from panic. The compiler can then treat the code after a call such as the one in adoptBootContext (tcb.cpp:71) as reached only when the check passed. In a function that returns a value, it also avoids a warning about a missing return after the panic.

    Neither function may be called from user mode. __printf takes a lock, and in xv6 the lock code reads sstatus to save the interrupt state. Reading sstatus in user mode is an illegal instruction, so the calling thread would fault and be killed. User code prints only through putc. If a drill asks you to print something from user-side code (the C API, the C++ API, a test), use putc or the tests' printString, never __printf.

    h/riscv.hpp: the supervisor registers

    h/riscv.hpp74 lines · in the submission zip as inc/riscv.hpp

    This class is the kernel's only direct access to the control and status registers (CSRs). It has no state and cannot be constructed. It is a named collection of one-instruction functions and bit constants.

    The warning in the class comment (lines 18–20) matters. Inside a trap handler, writing sepc or sstatus directly does nothing lasting, because trapEntry reloads both registers from the trap frame on the way out. A handler that wants to change where the thread resumes changes frame.sepc instead. trapHandler does exactly that for system calls (trap.cpp:93).

    Every bit the kernel refers to by name:

    Constant Bit Meaning
    SSTATUS_SIE 1 supervisor interrupt enable, while in supervisor mode. User mode ignores it: interrupts are always taken in user mode if sie allows them
    SSTATUS_SPIE 5 the value SIE had before the last trap; sret copies it back into SIE
    SSTATUS_SPP 8 the mode the last trap came from: 0 = user, 1 = supervisor. sret returns to this mode
    SIP_SSIP / SIE_SSIE 1 software interrupt pending / enabled. On this platform the machine-mode timer handler raises it, so for us it is the timer
    SIE_STIE 5 supervisor timer interrupt enable
    SIP_SEIP / SIE_SEIE 9 external interrupt (the console, through the PLIC) pending / enabled
    SCAUSE_INTERRUPT 63 set in scause when the trap is an interrupt rather than an exception

    The scause codes on lines 39–43 are the exception codes the kernel tells apart: 2 illegal instruction, 5 load access fault, 7 store access fault, 8 ecall from user mode, 9 ecall from supervisor mode.

    The casts in (uint64) 1 << 63 matter. A bare 1 is an int, and shifting a 32-bit int by 63 is undefined behaviour. Casting first makes it a 64-bit shift.

    Each accessor is a single CSR instruction wrapped in GCC's extended asm syntax:

    • csrr rd, csr reads a CSR. "=r"(v) asks the compiler for any general register to receive the result.
    • csrw csr, rs writes a whole CSR.
    • csrs csr, rs sets the bits that are 1 in rs, and csrc csr, rs clears them. They are read-modify-write in one instruction, so no other bit is disturbed. The kernel uses mc_sie to mask interrupts and mc_sip to acknowledge the timer.

    volatile matters most for the readers (r_). Without it, the compiler may treat an asm with an output as a pure computation: it could merge two reads of sip into one, or delete a read whose result it thinks is unused. An asm with no outputs, like the writers (w_, ms_, mc_), is treated as volatile anyway, so there the keyword only states the intent. volatile does not order the asm against ordinary memory accesses. That would need a "memory" clobber, and none of these accessors needs one, because no CSR here changes how the surrounding C++ code accesses memory.

    The prefixes follow one convention: r_ reads, w_ writes, ms_ sets a mask of bits, mc_ clears a mask of bits.

    Header-only, static, and with accessors nobody calls. Each function is one instruction, so a real call would cost more than the work. Defined in the class body, they are implicitly inline. The kernel uses only w_stvec, mc_sie, r_scause, r_stval and mc_sip. The rest (r_sstatus, ms_sie, r_sepc …) were kept on purpose, because the class is meant to be one complete interface to the hardware. A live modification that enables an interrupt source, or reads sepc for a debug print, then finds its accessor already written. A review suggested deleting the unused ones; that suggestion was not taken.

    The private constructor on line 69 is declared and never defined. It stops anyone creating a Riscv object, which would mean nothing. The same pattern appears in System, Scheduler, MemoryAllocator, Trap, Syscalls, kernel::Console and SlotAllocator.

    Questions

    Q6What is the difference between sstatus.SIE and the sie register?

    sie has one enable bit per interrupt source: SSIE (software/timer), STIE (timer), SEIE (external). sstatus.SIE is a global switch that applies only while the processor runs in supervisor mode. In user mode the global switch is ignored, and an interrupt is taken whenever its source bit in sie is set and it is pending in sip. That is why this kernel masks interrupts by clearing the bits in sie (system.cpp:37). Leaving sstatus.SIE at 0 would not be enough.

    Q7What does SPP hold, and who writes it?

    The hardware writes it on every trap: 0 if the trap came from user mode, 1 if from supervisor mode. sret reads it to choose the mode it returns to, and then sets it back to 0. The kernel sets it deliberately in one place: threadStart clears it, so that the first sret of a new thread lands in user mode (asm_routines.cpp:178–180). Apart from that, trapEntry's epilogue writes the whole sstatus, SPP included, back from the trap frame before every sret. That is why each thread's SPP survives a switch (asm_routines.cpp:73–74).

    Q8Why do the CSR accessors use __asm__ volatile?

    A CSR read can return a different value each time (sip changes under the program's feet), and the compiler cannot see that. volatile stops it from treating a read as a pure computation it may merge with another read or delete. The writers have no outputs, so GCC treats them as volatile anyway.

    Q9Why are all these classes static-only with a private constructor?

    Each one models something that exists exactly once in the system: the CPU's registers, the allocator, the scheduler, the trap mechanism. A static class says that directly, with no object to construct. A global object whose constructor is not constexpr would also need a dynamic initialiser, which nothing in this kernel runs (the one global object, Scheduler::ready, has a constexpr constructor for exactly that reason). The private constructor turns an accidental Riscv r; into a compile error.

    Q10Why does the kernel have its own error codes instead of just returning −1?

    The assignment only requires "negative on error". Distinct codes let the tests and a user tell apart a bad handle, lack of memory and a semaphore closed while waiting. That last one matters, because the assignment requires that sem_wait fail when the semaphore is closed under it.

  • Boot and shutdown
    • <

    This chapter follows the processor from the moment hw.lib hands over to the moment QEMU exits. Three functions carry the whole life of the system: System::initialize, System::run and System::halt. main() calls them in that order.

    Before main: what hw.lib has already done

    hw.lib is a stripped-down xv6 boot layer. Its _entry, at 0x80000000, sets up a boot stack called stack0. Its start() runs in machine mode: it delegates exceptions and interrupts to supervisor mode, programs the timer, opens memory protection (PMP) for the whole address space in every mode, and sets sie bits for the software, timer and external interrupts. It then executes mret into system_main(), now in supervisor mode. system_main initialises hw.lib's own parts and calls userinit(), which calls our main(). So main begins in supervisor mode, on stack0, with paging off.

    The call chain was read from hw.lib's objects with nm: main is referenced from proc.o, whose userinit is called by system_main in main.o. The comment in main.cpp says system_main calls main(), which is true only by way of userinit.

    Three things hw.lib leaves behind matter to us. Interrupt enables in sie, which we clear (below). A machine-mode timer that raises sip.SSIP ten times a second for as long as the machine runs, which we tolerate (chapter 6). PMP that lets user mode read, write and execute all of memory, which is why user mode's only restriction is privileged instructions.

    src/main.cpp

    src/main.cpp20 lines · in the submission zip as src/main.cpp

    hw.lib is compiled C, and it calls a symbol named exactly main. extern "C" says so explicitly. Strictly, GCC never mangles a function called main anyway (void main() without extern "C" still produces the symbol main), so the declaration documents the contract rather than changing the symbol. The return type is void because nothing reads a return value, and the function never returns anyway: halt() stops the emulator.

    h/system.hpp

    h/system.hpp44 lines · in the submission zip as inc/system.hpp

    EMULATOR_STOP_ADDRESS and EMULATOR_STOP_CODE are the one piece of platform knowledge this class holds. QEMU's virt machine has a small test device at 0x100000. Writing 0x5555 to it makes QEMU exit with status 0. The assignment names this as the way to end the program regularly.

    src/system.cpp

    src/system.cpp95 lines · in the submission zip as src/system.cpp

    userMain is defined by the tests (test/userMain.cpp), so it is only declared here. userMainBody adapts it to the thread-body signature void (*)(void *). The anonymous namespace gives it internal linkage: no other file can see it or clash with it.

    userMainBody sits in a kernel source file but runs in user mode, like every thread body. A function's mode is not a property of the file it is in. threadStart enters threadWrapper with sret and SPP = 0, and everything that threadWrapper calls then runs in user mode, whichever file it comes from.

    initialize(): four steps, in an order that matters

    Step 1 (line 37): mask interrupts, by clearing their sources in sie. This has to be done actively. In user mode sstatus.SIE is ignored: an interrupt whose source bit is set in sie and which is pending in sip is taken regardless. hw.lib has set the three source bits, and the machine-mode timer keeps raising SSIP. So the very first sret into user mode would take a timer interrupt at once. Clearing SSIE, STIE and SEIE makes "no interrupt source is enabled" literally true. SSIP then stays pending for ever, which is harmless because nothing is listening.

    Step 2 (line 39): the memory allocator before anything allocates. Step 4 creates a _thread with new, which asks SlotAllocator<_thread> for a slot. The first request makes it take a chunk from MemoryAllocator, and that only works once the free list exists.

    Step 3 (line 40): the trap vector. stvec must point at trapEntry before any user code runs, because a system call or a fault arriving before then would jump to wherever stvec pointed before.

    Step 4 (line 41): the boot flow of control becomes the main thread. adoptBootContext wraps the code that is running right now, on stack0, in a _thread and makes it running. The first dispatch() then has an "old" thread to save the context of.

    run(): start userMain, then idle until the end

    Lines 52–61: the first user thread is made the way thread_create makes every thread, except that kernel code calls kernel functions directly. It takes 64 blocks (4096 bytes) from MemoryAllocator, passes the block's end as the stack top, and calls _thread::create. It cannot use mem_alloc or thread_create: those are user-side functions that execute ecall. An ecall from supervisor mode arrives with scause 9, which the trap handler treats as a kernel bug (chapter 6).

    Lines 68–83: the main thread doubles as the idle thread. It loops for as long as any user thread is alive. Each time round it gives the processor away with _thread::dispatch(). It sits in the ready queue like any other thread, so it gets a turn once per round of the FCFS queue, sees the count still above zero, and passes the turn on again.

    Lines 77–80: deadlock is reported, not sat through. When the main thread is running, it is not in the ready queue. If the queue is also empty, no user thread is READY. Yet userThreadCount() > 0 says some are alive, so every one of them is BLOCKED on a semaphore. No thread is left that could signal one, and with no interrupts nothing else can wake them. So this is a deadlock in the user program, and the kernel says so with a panic.

    Why panic and not halt? Halting writes 0x5555, which means "every thread finished normally". A deadlocked program has not finished, so halting would make a failure look like a success. panic prints the message and spins, and the emulator stays up.

    A thread waiting in getc for a key is not a deadlock. It stays READY and re-tries on every turn (chapter 10), so the queue is never empty while it waits. Public test 7 is not a deadlock either. userMain keeps calling thread_dispatch() while it waits for the killed thread B, so it stays READY. The system just never finishes, which is what the faculty's instructions say to expect.

    When the loop ends, every user thread has ended: it called thread_exit, returned from its body, or was killed by a fault, which goes through the same _thread::exit(). run() returns into main(), which halts.

    halt()

    A volatile store, so the compiler must emit it exactly once and exactly here. The loop after it never actually runs, because QEMU has stopped. It is there because the function is documented not to return, and it gives the compiler something to assume about what follows. The empty __asm__ volatile ("") counts as a side effect. Without it, C++11 lets the compiler assume a side-effect-free loop terminates, and it might remove the loop.

    In every sandbox run of public tests 1–4, QEMU exits by itself with status 0 right after the last TEST n (...) line. The harness reports this as "the kernel halted the emulator - regular termination".

    Questions

    Q11Who calls main(), in which mode, and on which stack?

    hw.lib's supervisor-mode start-up code: start() drops from machine to supervisor mode with mret into system_main(), which calls userinit(), which calls main(). So main runs in supervisor mode, on hw.lib's boot stack stack0, with paging off. The main thread keeps that stack for its whole life: adoptBootContext gives it no stack of its own (tcb.cpp:23–26).

    Q12Why is main declared extern "C"?

    hw.lib is compiled C code that calls a symbol named exactly main, and extern "C" states that contract: C linkage, no C++ name mangling. For main specifically GCC would not mangle the name anyway, so the declaration is about making the contract explicit, which also matters for every other function called from hw.lib or from assembly.

    Q13What would go wrong if main simply called userMain() itself?

    userMain would run in supervisor mode on the boot stack. Its first C API call would execute ecall from supervisor mode (scause 9), which this kernel treats as a kernel bug and panics on. Even without that, public test 7 would fail. It checks that user code cannot read sepc, and in supervisor mode it could. And no thread would be left to count finished threads and halt at the end.

    Q14Why must interrupts be masked through sie and not just by leaving sstatus.SIE at 0?

    sstatus.SIE only gates interrupts while running in supervisor mode. In user mode it is ignored, and any interrupt enabled in sie and pending in sip is taken. hw.lib enables three sources and its timer keeps SSIP pending, so the first sret into user mode would trap at once. Clearing the bits in sie is the only mask that holds in user mode.

    Q15Why does MemoryAllocator::initialize() come before adoptBootContext()?

    adoptBootContext does new _thread(), and _thread's own operator new takes a slot from SlotAllocator<_thread>. The first time, that needs a chunk from MemoryAllocator, whose free list does not exist until initialize() builds it.

    Q16How does the program end regularly?

    Every thread ends in _thread::exit(): through thread_exit, called directly or by threadWrapper when the body returns, or through the fault path. That decrements the live-thread count (tcb.cpp:101). When the count reaches 0, the main thread's loop in System::run ends, run() returns into main(), and halt() writes 0x5555 to 0x100000, which makes QEMU exit.

    Q17What does the kernel do if all user threads are blocked on semaphores?

    The main thread notices on its next turn: the ready queue is empty although user threads are alive. It panics with "every user thread is blocked on a semaphore - deadlock". It does not halt, because halting signals a regular end. This was checked with a deliberate two-thread deadlock (SUITE=deadlock in the sandbox).

    Q18The main thread takes a turn every round. Is that not wasteful?

    It costs one extra context switch per round of the ready queue, which is negligible for these tests. The PDF's advice is an idle thread that runs only when nothing else is ready. That advice is not binding, and it would only save that one switch. Chapter 8 has a drill that makes the change: five lines in _thread::dispatch.

    Q19Why does userMain's stack come from MemoryAllocator::allocateBlocks and not from mem_alloc?

    mem_alloc is a user-side function that executes ecall. The kernel never issues system calls to itself. From supervisor mode that ecall would arrive as scause 9 and panic. The kernel uses its allocator directly and hands _thread::create exactly what thread_create would: the top of a 4096-byte block.

    start="4">
  • Memory: the allocator and slot storage (zadatak 1)
    • <

    Two allocators live in the kernel. MemoryAllocator is zadatak 1 itself: it manages the whole heap, and it is what mem_alloc and mem_free reach through the system call. SlotAllocator<T> sits on top of it and serves the kernel's own objects (_thread and _sem) in fixed-size slots, so the kernel never has to call its own system call.

    mem_alloc(size) allocates at least size bytes, rounded up to whole blocks of MEM_BLOCK_SIZE (64) and aligned to a block. It returns nullptr on failure. mem_free(ptr) returns 0 or a negative code. For a pointer that did not come from mem_alloc the behaviour is undefined, and "jezgro može vratiti grešku ukoliko može da je detektuje". Across the ABI, mem_alloc's argument is a number of blocks, not bytes. The PDF leaves the algorithm open: first fit or best fit, continuous allocation, and free fragments are to be merged.

    The idea in one picture

    The heap is a run of segments laid end to end, with no gaps. Each segment spends its first whole block on a header and hands the rest out as payload. Free segments are also linked into a list sorted by address.

    h/memory_allocator.hpp

    h/memory_allocator.hpp99 lines · in the submission zip as inc/memory_allocator.hpp

    The interface counts in blocks, because the ABI does. blocksFor(bytes) is the one place inside the kernel where bytes are rounded up to blocks: (bytes + 63) / 64. isAllocated exists for exactly one caller, _thread::create. That function is about to write a thread's first context into a block the user handed over, and checks first that the block really is a live allocation of the right size.

    The header is three words: 24 bytes. It gets a whole 64-byte block anyway, for two reasons:

    • The payload comes out block-aligned for free. The heap is rounded to block boundaries (below), every segment is a whole number of blocks, so every header starts on a block boundary and every payload starts one block later.
    • The header is found by subtracting exactly one block. No stored offset, no size field to read first. allocatedSegment does payload - 64 and checks what it finds.

    It costs nothing extra. A 24-byte header packed in front of n blocks of payload would need 24 + 64n bytes, which rounds up to n + 1 blocks anyway. The magic words catch pointers that never came from the allocator, which the assignment explicitly allows us to reject. MAGIC_ALLOCATED spells "allocated" in hex (0A110CA7ED) and MAGIC_FREE spells "free" (F2EE). Both are values that are unlikely to occur in a header by accident. User data could contain them, but user data never sits where a header is looked for unless a pointer is wrong.

    MIN_SPLIT_BLOCKS = 2: when a free segment is larger than a request, the leftover is split off as a new free segment only if it has at least a header and one payload block. A one-block leftover would be a header with no payload: findable, never usable. Leaving it attached to the allocation keeps the invariant that every segment on the free list can serve some request.

    src/memory_allocator.cpp

    src/memory_allocator.cpp147 lines · in the submission zip as src/memory_allocator.cpp

    The three static members are initialised with constants (nullptr), so they need no start-up code. That rule appears again and again (chapter 13, invariant 9): this kernel never runs dynamic initialisers. addressOf is the single place where block arithmetic becomes a byte address.

    initialize()

    HEAP_START_ADDR is not block-aligned. It is the address right after the kernel image, 0x8000d190 in the sandbox build. So the low bound is rounded up to the next multiple of 64 and the high bound down. The integer arithmetic (x + 63) / 64 * 64 rounds up; x / 64 * 64 rounds down. After this, the heap is a whole number of blocks and the whole heap is one free segment.

    Measured in the sandbox with the drill in chapter 7, in a build whose test program is tiny: when userMain starts, the free payload is 134,176,768 bytes, about 128 MiB. By then the boot has taken a chunk of 16 thread slots and userMain's stack. The exact figure depends on how large the kernel image is, because the heap starts right after it.

    allocateBlocks(): first fit

    Line by line:

    • Line 47 refuses a request of 0 blocks and anything at least as large as the whole heap. The second test also guarantees that blocks + HEADER_BLOCKS on line 49 cannot overflow, even for a wild block count sent through the raw ABI, such as __syscall(abi::MEM_ALLOC, ~0UL, 0, 0, 0). (Through the C API, mem_alloc((size_t) -1) never gets that far: the rounding (size + 63) / 64 wraps around to 0 blocks, which the first test refuses.)
    • Line 49: the segment must hold the payload plus its own header.
    • Lines 51–53 walk the free list with a trailing previous pointer. That pointer is needed because the list is singly linked, and unlinking a node means changing its predecessor's nextFree.
    • Line 55: first fit takes the first segment that is large enough.
    • Lines 58–68 split off the tail when it is large enough to be useful (at least 2 blocks). The leftover gets its own header, inherits the segment's place in the list (leftover->nextFree = segment->nextFree), and becomes the node that replaces the segment in the list. Taking the head of the segment and leaving the tail keeps the list sorted by address without re-inserting anything.
    • Lines 70–71 unlink: either the predecessor now points past the segment, or the segment was the head of the list.
    • Lines 73–75 mark the segment allocated, clear its stale link, and return the address one block past the header.

    A worked example: mem_alloc(100) in the C API computes (100 + 63) / 64 = 2 blocks and sends 2 through the ABI. The kernel needs 2 + 1 = 3 blocks. It takes them from the first free segment of at least 3, splits off the rest, and returns segment + 64. The caller gets 128 usable bytes, block-aligned.

    Recognising our own pointers

    This is how mem_free detects a pointer it did not hand out. The checks run in an order that guarantees nothing is read from memory until the address is known to lie inside the heap. A wild pointer can therefore not make the kernel itself fault. A fault in supervisor mode would stop the whole system.

    1. null → no;
    2. not a multiple of 64 → cannot be a payload we returned;
    3. the header address (one block down) must lie inside [heapLow, heapHigh);
    4. only now is it read: the magic must say ALLOCATED, which rejects a double free, a pointer into the middle of a payload that happens to be 64-aligned, and most wild pointers;
    5. the size must be sane: more than just a header, and not running past the end of the heap.

    isAllocated adds one question on top: is the payload at least bytes long?

    Line 92 casts away const ((Segment *) ((const char *) payload - …)). The function finds the header that belongs to a payload pointer. freeBlocks then writes to that header, while isAllocated only reads it. One function serves both.

    freeBlocks(): insert in address order, then merge

    After validation, the segment is marked FREE and put back into the list at the position its address dictates. The walk stops at the first free segment above it, so previous is the free segment just below it and next the one just above. Those are the only two segments it could possibly touch in memory.

    Why forward first: mergeIfAdjacent(segment, next) may grow segment to cover next. mergeIfAdjacent(previous, segment) may then grow previous to cover the already-enlarged segment. Done the other way round, a backward merge would absorb segment into previous, and the forward merge would then have to be written as mergeIfAdjacent(previous, next), but only in the case where the backward merge happened. The forward-first order handles all four cases (no neighbour, lower neighbour, upper neighbour, both) with the same two unconditional calls.

    Two segments merge only if the first ends exactly where the second begins (addressOf(low, low->blocks) == high). The absorbed header's magic is zeroed. A stale pointer to it, such as a second mem_free of an address that was merged away, then fails the magic check instead of corrupting the list.

    Checked by the own tests in the sandbox: the heap filled with 1 MiB blocks, then all of them freed, coalesces back into one block large enough for a request that only fits if every free merged. A double free, mem_free(nullptr) and a pointer into the middle of a block are all rejected with a negative code.

    h/slot_allocator.hpp: storage for kernel objects

    h/slot_allocator.hpp145 lines · in the submission zip as inc/slot_allocator.hpp

    The kernel creates _thread and _sem objects on behalf of user code. It cannot use the global new, because that one is wired to mem_alloc, a system call. It could call MemoryAllocator::allocateBlocks for each object, but a 40-byte _thread would then cost a 64-byte header plus a 64-byte payload block, and thousands of tiny segments would be scattered through the heap. So objects of one class are grouped into chunks of 16 slots.

    A free slot's own storage holds the link to the next free slot (FreeSlot { FreeSlot *next; }), so the free list costs no memory at all. allocate takes from the head. deallocate appends at the tail, which makes the list first in, first out. Line 71 writes the link into the slot's first word, which is the property chapter 9 builds on: once an object is destroyed, its first word is always overwritten with a link (another slot's address, or null).

    owns walks the chunks and compares numbers only. It never reads memory at address, so any value at all, including garbage from user code, can be asked about safely. It answers yes only for the exact start of a slot. _sem::fromHandle uses it to vet a semaphore handle before reading anything through it.

    The sizes work out as follows:

    Class sizeof(T) slot chunk bytes blocks from MemoryAllocator
    _thread 40 48 16 + 16 × 48 = 784 13 payload + 1 header = 14
    _sem 32 32 16 + 16 × 32 = 528 9 payload + 1 header = 10

    slotSize() rounds up to 16 bytes, and the 16-byte chunk header keeps the first slot 16-byte aligned, because the chunk itself starts on a 64-byte block. grow() threads all 16 new slots onto the free list through deallocate, lowest address first, so they are handed out in address order.

    These definitions are in the header, which is normally an ODR violation for static data members. Here it is correct, because they are members of a class template: the linker keeps one copy per instantiation (SlotAllocator<_thread>, SlotAllocator<_sem>), however many files include the header. Their initialisers are nullptr, so again no start-up code is needed.

    A class that uses slot storage must declare its operator new noexcept. For an operator new that may throw, the C++ rules let the compiler assume the result is never null and run the constructor on it unconditionally. When the slots and the heap are exhausted, allocate() returns nullptr, and the constructor would write to address 0. With noexcept the compiler inserts the nullptr check and new evaluates to nullptr, which _thread::create and _sem::open turn into SYS_ERR_NO_MEMORY.

    Questions

    Q20Which algorithm does your allocator use, and why that one?

    First fit over a free list sorted by address, with splitting and coalescing on both sides. The PDF allows first fit or best fit. First fit is the simplest to explain and change, and it is fast when the free list is short. Sorting by address is what makes coalescing cheap. The drill at the end of this chapter turns it into best fit in about 20 lines.

    Q21Why does every allocation spend a whole 64-byte block on a 24-byte header?

    The payload comes out block-aligned, and the header is found from the payload by subtracting exactly one block. It also costs nothing: 24 + 64n bytes round up to n + 1 blocks anyway.

    Q22What does mem_free do with a pointer that did not come from mem_alloc?

    It checks, in this order: not null, 64-aligned, header address inside the heap, and only then, reading the header, magic word says ALLOCATED and size sane. Nothing is read before the header is known to lie inside the heap, and nothing is written before all checks pass. Any failure returns SYS_ERR_BAD_ARGUMENT. The assignment calls this case undefined and allows an error where it can be detected. A double free fails because the magic changed to FREE, or to 0 if the segment was merged away.

    Q23How does mem_alloc(100) travel through the system, in blocks?

    The C API rounds 100 bytes up to 2 blocks and passes 2 in a1. The kernel needs 3 blocks (one for the header), takes them from the first free segment that has at least 3, splits off the rest if it is at least 2 blocks, and returns the address one block past the header. The caller has 128 usable bytes.

    Q24Why is the free list sorted by address?

    So that freeing finds both physical neighbours during the same walk that finds the insertion point: previous ends right below the freed segment and next starts right above it. Coalescing is then two address comparisons. An unsorted list would need a search for each neighbour, or a second list of all segments.

    Q25What fragmentation does your allocator have?

    Internal: up to 63 bytes lost to rounding up to a block, plus the one-block header, plus at most one block when a 1-block leftover is not split off. External: holes between live segments. It is reduced by merging every freed segment with its free neighbours, but not eliminated, since nothing moves live segments.

    Q26Is the allocator thread-safe?

    It has no locks and needs none. No interrupt is ever enabled, and threads switch only inside _thread::dispatch(), never in the middle of an allocator function. So exactly one flow of control is inside the kernel at any time. With preemption inside the kernel this would change.

    Q27How does the kernel allocate its own objects, and why not with mem_alloc or the global new?

    With SlotAllocator<T>: chunks of 16 slots, each chunk one MemoryAllocator request, with free slots linked through themselves. The global new calls mem_alloc, which executes ecall, and the kernel would trap into itself (an ecall from supervisor mode, which panics here). Per-object segments would also waste a header block each and fragment the heap.

    Q28Why is the slot allocator's free list FIFO and not the simpler LIFO?

    So that a freed slot is reused as late as possible. A stale semaphore handle then keeps pointing at a free slot, which _sem::fromHandle recognises and refuses, for as long as possible. With LIFO, the very next sem_open would get the slot just freed, and a stale handle would silently name the new semaphore.

    Q29Why must _thread::operator new be noexcept?

    Only for a non-throwing operator new does the compiler check the returned pointer for nullptr before running the constructor. Without noexcept it assumes success and would construct the object at address 0 when memory runs out.

    Q30Why are SlotAllocator's static members defined in the header?

    They belong to a class template. Each instantiation's statics are emitted wherever they are used, and the linker merges the copies. It is the normal way to define template statics, and their constant initialisers need no start-up code.

    Q31Are slot chunks ever returned to the heap?

    No. Kernel objects come and go, but the slots get reused, and returning a chunk would need a scan to prove all 16 slots are free. The cost is small: 14 blocks per 16 threads and 10 blocks per 16 semaphores, at the peak count.

    Drill

    Drill 1Change the allocator from first fit to best fit

    Task. "Your allocator is first fit. Make it best fit." Only MemoryAllocator::allocateBlocks changes. Splitting, unlinking and marking stay as they are. What changes is which segment is chosen. Walk the whole free list and remember the smallest segment that is large enough, together with its predecessor, because the list is singly linked. An exact fit cannot be beaten, so the walk may stop there.

    Where: src/memory_allocator.cpp, allocateBlocks (the first-fit loop, memory_allocator.cpp:51–78), and the one-word class comment in h/memory_allocator.hpp.

    Watch out for: the predecessor. Keeping only best and then trying to unlink it fails, because nothing points back to the node before it. The break inside the for skips the loop's increment expression, which is fine here because previous was already saved.

    Test. Make two holes: an 11-block one lower in the heap, a 4-block one higher up. Then ask for 3 blocks, which with the header needs 4 and fits both. First fit takes the lower hole, best fit the exact one:

    The test program used: put it in test/userMain.cpp of a scratch copy of the project, in place of the public tests' userMain
    #include "../h/syscall_c.h"

namespace
{
void print(const char *text) { while (*text != '\0') { putc(*text++); } }
}

void userMain()
{
    /* Two holes: 11 blocks lower in the heap, then 4 blocks higher up. */
    void *big = mem_alloc(10 * MEM_BLOCK_SIZE);
    void *fence1 = mem_alloc(1);
    void *small = mem_alloc(3 * MEM_BLOCK_SIZE);
    void *fence2 = mem_alloc(1);
    mem_free(big);
    mem_free(small);

    /* Needs 3 payload blocks + 1 header = 4: fits both holes. */
    void *p = mem_alloc(3 * MEM_BLOCK_SIZE);
    if (p == small) { print("best fit: the request went into the 4-block hole\n"); }
    else if (p == big) { print("first fit: the request went into the first hole that fits\n"); }
    else { print("neither hole was used\n"); }

    mem_free(p);
    mem_free(fence1);
    mem_free(fence2);
}

    Run in the sandbox (GCC 9.4): the unmodified kernel printed "first fit: the request went into the first hole that fits". The patched kernel printed "best fit: the request went into the 4-block hole". The own test suite still passes on the patched kernel (84 of 84 checks).

    start="5">
  • The user side: the ABI and the C API
    • <

    Everything in this chapter runs in user mode. The C API is a thin layer: each function arranges its arguments the way the ABI wants them and executes ecall through one shared stub, __syscall. Only two functions do more, and the assignment tells them to.

    The ABI: a system call is made with ecall. a0 holds the call's code, a1, a2, … hold the arguments from left to right, and the result comes back in a0. Every ABI call has exactly the C API's signature and meaning, "osim" two: mem_alloc passes a number of blocks, and thread_create takes a fourth argument, stack_space, a stack the C API has already allocated, "na čiju poslednju lokaciju ukazuje stack_space".

    h/abi.hpp: the contract between the two sides

    h/abi.hpp71 lines · in the submission zip as inc/abi.hpp

    Apart from the faculty's hw.h, this header and error_codes.hpp are the only two project headers both sides of the boundary include. The C API uses them to make calls, the kernel's dispatcher uses them to decode calls, and neither side includes the other's internals.

    The codes are the PDF's table: memory in 0x0_, threads in 0x1_, semaphores in 0x2_, time in 0x3_, console in 0x4_. The enum's underlying type is uint64, the width of a register, so a code travels through a0 and is compared against the saved frame.a0 without conversions.

    __syscall is the user side's only way into the kernel. The RISC-V calling convention passes a function's first five integer arguments in a0…a4. That is exactly the register layout the ABI asks for, so when the C API calls __syscall(code, x, y, z, w), the compiler has already put everything where the kernel expects it before the first instruction of __syscall runs. Its body is therefore ecall; ret and nothing else (chapter 6). Unused arguments are passed as 0.

    threadWrapper is where every new thread starts, in user mode. It is declared here because the kernel needs its address: threadStart, in assembly, jumps to it by name. That is also why it has C linkage: assembly could name a mangled C++ function, but the mangled name (something like _Z13threadWrapperPFvPvES_) is unreadable and changes with the signature. C linkage gives it the stable name threadWrapper. It is defined on the user side, below.

    h/syscall_c.h and h/syscall_c.hpp: the C API as declared

    h/syscall_c.h68 lines · in the submission zip as inc/syscall_c.h

    The two handle types are pointers to classes the user never sees defined. The forward declarations are enough to pass pointers around, which is all user code does with them. In the kernel, _thread and _sem are the real control block and semaphore (chapters 8 and 9).

    Each declaration carries its ABI code as a comment, so the table and the header can be compared line by line. EOF is required by the C API table. This console cannot fail, so getc never returns it. static const at namespace scope gives it internal linkage, so each file that includes the header gets its own copy with no link conflict.

    h/syscall_c.hpp10 lines · in the submission zip as inc/syscall_c.hpp

    The assignment text calls the header syscall_c.hpp, while the public tests #include "../h/syscall_c.h". Both names exist so that either works. The real content lives in the .h, because that is the one the tests use.

    src/syscall_c.cpp: the C API as implemented

    src/syscall_c.cpp127 lines · in the submission zip as src/syscall_c.cpp

    Memory

    mem_alloc(0) returns nullptr without a system call: there is nothing to allocate, and the kernel would refuse 0 blocks anyway. Otherwise bytes are rounded up to blocks: (size + 63) / 64. The kernel returns the payload pointer in a0, or 0 on failure, and the cast turns it back into a pointer.

    The same rounding exists in the kernel as MemoryAllocator::blocksFor. The C API does not call that function, because user code stays on its side of the ABI and includes nothing from the kernel but abi.hpp and the error codes. Two copies of a one-line formula are the price of a clean boundary.

    Threads, and where every thread starts

    thread_create is the one function with real logic, and the order matters:

    1. A null handle is refused before anything is allocated (line 36). The kernel checks it too, but refusing here saves allocating and freeing a stack.
    2. The stack comes from mem_alloc, which is itself a system call. So thread_create costs two traps: one for the stack, one for the thread.
    3. stack_space is the block's end, stack + DEFAULT_STACK_SIZE (line 46). The stack grows downward and sp is decremented before the first store, so the first sp is one past the last byte. This is the project's reading of the PDF's "poslednja lokacija". Taken literally, the last location would be the last byte, base + 4095, which is not a valid initial sp (it is not 16-aligned). The ambiguity and this resolution are recorded in docs/SPECIFICATION.md, section 9.
    4. If the kernel refuses, the stack is freed again (line 49). Until the call succeeds, the block belongs to the caller. After a success, it belongs to the kernel, which frees it together with the thread (chapter 8).

    thread_exit returns only if the kernel refuses the exit, which happens only for the main thread. The main thread never runs this code, so for every caller of this function it never returns. thread_dispatch ignores the SYS_OK the kernel leaves in a0, because its signature is void.

    This is the first user-mode code every thread runs. The kernel's threadStart puts body in a0 and arg in a1 and executes sret to this address. To the compiler it is an ordinary function called with two arguments. It calls the body, and when the body returns it calls thread_exit(). So a body that simply returns ends its thread, and a body that calls thread_exit() itself never comes back here. There is nothing to return to: threadWrapper was never called. Its ra still holds the address of threadStart, left over from the switch that started the thread. If threadWrapper ever did return, it would jump there in user mode and fault on threadStart's first CSR instruction.

    Why the body and argument come in registers. The alternatives were letting threadWrapper read them from the kernel's _thread object, which is possible because PMP lets user mode read all of memory, but puts user code inside kernel data structures, or an extra system call to fetch them, which costs a trap per thread and adds a code outside the assignment's table. Carrying them in the new thread's first context costs two mv instructions in threadStart (chapter 8). Decided with Aleksandar on 2026-09-20.

    Semaphores, time and console

    sem_open refuses a null handle locally, like thread_create. Everything else passes straight through: the kernel validates every handle itself (chapter 9), because anything a user program hands over must be checked in the kernel anyway. (int) narrows the 64-bit a0 to the C API's int. A negative code was sign-extended to 64 bits by the kernel, so it survives the cast unchanged.

    The kernel returns the character in a0 as an unsigned byte. putc passes its character as (uint64) (uint8) chr: zero-extended, so a character with the high bit set can never arrive in the kernel as a huge sign-extended number. On RISC-V char is unsigned anyway, but the double cast states the intent and does not depend on that. Waiting for the UART happens in the kernel, not here (chapter 10).

    Never let a C API or C++ API function use the registers t0–t6. Public test 1 does li t1, 7, calls thread_dispatch(), and reads t1 back. The compiler does not know t1 is live across that call. The calling convention lets any called function overwrite t0–t6, so the test passes only because the wrapper path happens not to use them. trapEntry restores t1 faithfully, but it would restore whatever the wrapper left there. The sandbox harness disassembles syscall_c.o and syscall_cpp.o on every build and fails if a t register appears. If you add code to these wrappers in a live modification (a loop, a local array, a call to a helper), public test 1 is the test to rerun.

    Questions

    Q32What exactly is your ABI?

    ecall, with the call's code in a0, the arguments in a1…a4 left to right, and the result in a0. Every other register comes back unchanged. The codes are the PDF's table (h/abi.hpp). It differs from the C API in two places only, as the PDF prescribes: MEM_ALLOC counts blocks, and THREAD_CREATE takes a fourth argument, the stack.

    Q33Why is __syscall only two instructions?

    The calling convention already puts a function's first five arguments in a0–a4, and those are the registers the ABI uses. By the time __syscall starts executing, the arguments are in place. All it does is ecall, and ret once the kernel has left the result in a0.

    Q34Who allocates a new thread's stack, who frees it, and what happens if thread_create fails?

    The C API allocates it with mem_alloc(DEFAULT_STACK_SIZE) before the ecall. If the kernel refuses the thread, the C API frees it again (syscall_c.cpp:49). If the thread is created, the kernel owns the block and frees it when the finished thread is released, at the next dispatch after it exits (chapter 8).

    Q35What does stack_space point to, and why there?

    One past the last byte of the block: base + 4096. The PDF says the stack is placed in a reserved space "na čiju poslednju lokaciju ukazuje stack_space". Read literally that would be the last byte, base + 4095, but that is not a usable initial sp: it is not 16-aligned, and sp is decremented before the first store. So the project reads it as the top of the stack, exactly the first value of sp. That is an interpretation, and worth saying so if asked. The kernel subtracts 4096 to find the block again, both to check it and to free it later.

    Q36What happens when a thread's body returns instead of calling thread_exit?

    It returns into threadWrapper, which then calls thread_exit() itself (syscall_c.cpp:68–72). So both ways of ending a thread go through the same system call. threadWrapper never returns, because nothing called it.

    Q37Why is threadWrapper on the user side rather than in the kernel?

    Everything it does is user work: call the body, call thread_exit. It must run in user mode, since the body is user code. The kernel only needs its address, to aim the new thread's first sret at it.

    Q38How does a negative error code survive the trip through a 64-bit register?

    The kernel's asResult casts the int code to long and then to uint64, which sign-extends it: −4 becomes 0xFFFF…FFFC. The C API's (int) cast takes the low 32 bits, which are 0xFFFFFFFC, −4 again.

    Q39Why must the C API functions not use t0–t6?

    Public test 1 sets t1 with inline assembly, calls thread_dispatch(), and expects t1 unchanged. The trap handler preserves every register across the ecall, but the wrapper code before the ecall runs first. Under the calling convention it may overwrite t1 freely. The compiled wrappers use no t register, and the sandbox harness checks that on every build.

    Q40Why do both syscall_c.h and syscall_c.hpp exist?

    The assignment text names the header syscall_c.hpp, while the public tests include syscall_c.h. The .h holds the declarations and the .hpp just includes it, so code written against either name compiles.

    Q41Can getc return EOF?

    No. The console here cannot fail: GETC waits until a character arrives. EOF is defined only because the C API table requires it.

    start="6">
  • The trap: from ecall to sret
    • <

    A trap is how the processor leaves user code: a system call (ecall), an exception (an illegal instruction, a bad address), or an interrupt. This kernel has exactly one entry point for all of them, trapEntry. This chapter covers what the hardware does, what trapEntry saves and why, and how trapHandler decides what the trap was.

    What the hardware does, and does not do

    On a trap into supervisor mode On sret
    sepc ← address of the trapping instruction pc ← sepc
    sstatus.SPP ← the mode it came from (0 user, 1 supervisor) mode ← SPP, then SPP ← 0
    sstatus.SPIE ← SIE, then SIE ← 0 SIE ← SPIE, then SPIE ← 1
    scause ← the cause; stval ← extra information, such as a bad address  
    pc ← stvec (direct mode: one address for everything)  

    Nothing else. No register is saved and the stack pointer does not change. sp still points into the stack the thread was using, which is exactly where this kernel wants to work (decision 1 in chapter 1). Saving everything else is trapEntry's job.

    h/trap_frame.hpp: what gets saved

    h/trap_frame.hpp79 lines · in the submission zip as inc/trap_frame.hpp

    The fields are in register-number order: ra is x1, then x3…x31, then the two CSRs. Two registers are left out:

    • x0 is hardwired to zero. There is nothing to save.
    • x2 (sp) points at the frame itself. It is restored by adding 256 back, not by loading it.

    Why the temporaries too? A normal function call may overwrite t0–t6 and a0–a7: the caller saves what it needs. A trap is not a normal call. The interrupted code did not choose to call anything. An exception or interrupt can happen between any two instructions. Even for ecall the ABI promises that nothing but a0 changes, and public test 1 checks it with t1. So everything user code can see is saved.

    Why sepc and sstatus? They are single global registers. While a thread is switched out inside the kernel, other threads trap and overwrite both. Each thread needs its own return address and its own SPP when it finally leaves through sret, so both travel in its frame.

    The assembly in trapEntry cannot see C++ constants. Its offsets are literal numbers. These static_asserts make the compiler check the struct against some of those numbers: the size, and the offsets of ra, t1, a0, a4, t6, sepc and sstatus. Adding or removing a field, or moving one of those seven, stops the build. Swapping two fields between the pinned ones, a1 with a2 say, would compile, and the dispatcher would silently read the wrong argument. Nothing checks the assembly itself either: a comment asks that it use the same numbers. __builtin_offsetof is GCC's built-in form of offsetof. The standard offsetof from <stddef.h> expands to it. The project simply includes no standard headers at all.

    h/asm_routines.hpp: declarations

    h/asm_routines.hpp102 lines · in the submission zip as inc/asm_routines.hpp

    The rest of this header (yield, threadStart, YieldFrame) belongs to the context switch and is covered in chapter 8.

    Naked functions instead of a .S file. __attribute__((naked)) tells GCC to emit no prologue and no epilogue: the function body is exactly the asm inside it. On the faculty's toolchain (binutils 2.34) a .S file would build too. binutils 2.42 rejects the -ggdb flag the Makefile passes to the assembler, but that does not affect the faculty VM. The naked form does not depend on the assembler's flags at all, and all the assembly sits in one C++ file. Two rules come with them. Only basic asm: GCC does not support operands (%0) in naked functions. lla, not la, for a different reason: la may assemble into a load from the global offset table when code is compiled position-independent, while lla always computes the address PC-relatively. This was a deliberate choice, confirmed with Aleksandar.

    src/asm_routines.cpp: __syscall and trapEntry

    src/asm_routines.cpp182 lines · in the submission zip as src/asm_routines.cpp

    __syscall is the whole user half of the ABI: ecall, then ret. Because the function is naked, ra still holds the return address into the C API function that called it, so ret goes straight back there. When the kernel has finished, it has already moved sepc 4 bytes past the ecall, so sret resumes at the ret, with the result in a0.

    • Line 29, aligned(4): stvec holds the handler address in its upper bits and the mode in its two lowest bits (0 = direct). The address must have those bits clear. Without the C extension every instruction is 4 bytes and every function is 4-aligned anyway. The attribute turns that coincidence into a guarantee.
    • Line 32 makes room for the frame on the current stack. There is no switch to a kernel stack and no sscratch. The kernel works on the stack of the thread that trapped.
    • Lines 34–63 store x1 and x3…x31. After this, every register may be used freely.
    • Lines 65–68 save sepc and sstatus. CSRs cannot be stored to memory directly, so they pass through t0, which is safe to overwrite because its user value was saved on line 37.
    • Lines 70–71 call trapHandler(frame) with a0 = sp, the frame's address. From here on it is ordinary C++ on the same stack, below the frame.

    When trapHandler returns, sp points at the same frame again: C++ functions leave sp as they found it. But much may have happened in between: the thread may have been switched out and run again much later. So:

    • Lines 73–76 reload sstatus and sepc from the frame, not from what the CSRs hold now. Other threads' traps have overwritten them since. This is also where the sepc += 4 that trapHandler wrote into the frame takes effect.
    • Lines 78–107 restore every register, including a0, into which the dispatcher wrote the result. t0 is restored here as well, after its last use as scratch on line 76.
    • Line 109 releases the frame, and line 110, sret, returns to the mode in SPP at the address in sepc.

    The offsets exist twice: in TrapFrame and as literals here. Change one, and you must change the other. The static_asserts catch a changed struct, but not a changed literal. The same warning applies to sepc and sstatus inside a handler: writing the live registers with Riscv::w_sepc has no lasting effect, because lines 73–76 overwrite them from the frame. Write frame.sepc instead.

    h/trap.hpp

    h/trap.hpp31 lines · in the submission zip as inc/trap.hpp

    trapHandler is declared outside the class with C linkage, because the assembly on line 71 calls it by its plain name.

    src/trap.cpp: what kind of trap was it?

    src/trap.cpp99 lines · in the submission zip as src/trap.cpp

    A fault is handled according to where it happened. That is read from SPP in the saved sstatus, the mode the trap came from:

    • From user mode, the fault is the thread's own doing. The report is printed, and the thread is ended exactly as if it had called thread_exit. _thread::exit() switches to another thread and never returns. This thread's frame, kernel frames and stack are abandoned where they lie and freed at the next dispatch (chapter 8). Public test 7 expects exactly this: thread B faults at i=10, never sets its finished flag, and the test's own wait loop never ends.
    • From supervisor mode, it is a bug in the kernel, and nothing can safely continue. panic prints and spins. It deliberately does not halt: halting writes 0x5555, the signal for a regular end, and a crashed kernel must not look like one.

    The report uses __printf, which is safe here because this code runs in supervisor mode. stval is read live, which is fine because nothing has trapped since this trap began.

    Why stval differs between the VM and the sandbox. For an illegal instruction, the RISC-V specification lets the hardware put either the faulting instruction's bits or zero into stval. The sandbox's QEMU 8.2 reports 0x14102ff3, which is the encoding of csrr t6, sepc. Your VM run of test 7 showed 0. The likely cause is an older QEMU on the VM, which does not fill stval in this case. The kernel only prints what it finds, so either value is correct. The value that matters is scause = 2.

    Three cases, tested in this order:

    1. Interrupt (bit 63 of scause). None should arrive, because every source is masked in sie. The only one this platform keeps raising is the timer's SSIP, so the handler acknowledges it by clearing that bit and returns. sepc is not touched, because an interrupt does not skip the interrupted instruction. This branch is where time slicing would go (chapter 8 has the drill).
    2. ecall from user mode (scause 8). frame->sepc += 4 first, because sepc points at the ecall itself and without the increment sret would execute it again, for ever. Then the dispatcher does the work.
    3. Anything else: an illegal instruction (2), a bad load (5), a bad store (7), an ecall from supervisor mode (9). All are faults. The kernel never executes ecall itself, so 9 can only mean a kernel bug.

    scause is read from the live register on line 71, before anything can switch threads. sepc is changed in the frame, because the frame is what the epilogue restores.

    Questions

    Q42Walk me through what happens between a thread executing ecall and continuing after it.

    Hardware: sepc ← the ecall's address, SPP ← 0, SPIE ← SIE, SIE ← 0, scause ← 8, jump to stvec = trapEntry. trapEntry pushes 256 bytes on the current stack, saves 30 registers plus sepc and sstatus, and calls trapHandler(frame). trapHandler sees scause 8, adds 4 to frame->sepc, and calls Syscalls::dispatch, which reads the code and arguments from the frame and writes the result into frame->a0. Back in trapEntry: sstatus and sepc are reloaded from the frame, every register is reloaded, sp goes up by 256, and sret returns to user mode at the instruction after the ecall.

    Q43The calling convention says t0–t6 are caller-saved. Why does trapEntry save them?

    A trap is not a call. An exception or interrupt can happen between any two instructions, where the interrupted code expects every register to keep its value. For ecall, the ABI promises that only a0 changes. Public test 1 checks it by reading t1 back after thread_dispatch().

    Q44Why are x0 and x2 not in the trap frame?

    x0 is always zero. x2 is sp, which points at the frame itself. It is restored by addi sp, sp, 256, not by a load.

    Q45Why does the frame include sepc and sstatus?

    A context switch can happen inside the trap handler. By the time a thread leaves through sret, other threads' traps have overwritten both registers. Each thread needs its own return address and its own SPP, so both are saved in its frame and reloaded just before sret.

    Q46Why is sepc advanced by 4 for ecall but not for a fault?

    For ecall, sepc points at the ecall itself, which has done its job. Returning there would repeat the system call for ever. For a fault the instruction did not complete. The handler either kills the thread, so it never returns, or, in a design that fixes the cause, retries the same instruction. Every instruction is 4 bytes because the build has no C extension (-march=rv64ima).

    Q47Why doesn't your trap entry use sscratch to switch stacks?

    It has no other stack to switch to. Kernel code deliberately runs on the trapping thread's own stack, so the hardware's untouched sp is already right. A design with one shared kernel stack, or with the kernel stack stored in sscratch, would need the swap.

    Q48What does "direct mode" in stvec mean, and why is trapEntry aligned to 4?

    The two lowest bits of stvec select the mode: 0 is direct, meaning every trap jumps to the same address, and 1 is vectored, meaning interrupts jump to base + 4 × cause. So the handler's address must have those bits clear, and aligned(4) guarantees that.

    Q49What happens in your kernel on a timer interrupt?

    None arrives: System::initialize clears SSIE, STIE and SEIE in sie. The machine-mode timer still sets sip.SSIP, but with SSIE clear it stays pending and is never delivered. If an interrupt did arrive, trapHandler would clear SSIP and return to the interrupted instruction.

    Q50Trace public test 7.

    Thread B, in user mode, executes csrr t6, sepc. User mode may not access sepc, so the hardware raises an illegal instruction exception: scause 2, sepc = that instruction, SPP = 0. trapEntry saves the frame. trapHandler finds neither an interrupt nor an ecall and calls handleFault, which prints the report, sees SPP = 0, and calls _thread::exit(). B is marked FINISHED and never runs again. A, C and D finish normally. userMain waits for B's flag for ever, so the program never ends regularly, as the test's instructions expect.

    Q51Why does a fault in supervisor mode panic instead of halting?

    Halting writes 0x5555 to 0x100000, the signal that every thread finished normally. A kernel fault is the opposite of that. panic prints and spins, so the failure is visible and the emulator stays up.

    Q52What is scause 9, and why is it a bug in your kernel?

    ecall from supervisor mode. Kernel code, including the main thread, calls kernel functions directly and never uses the system call interface. An ecall from supervisor mode can therefore only come from a kernel bug, such as kernel code calling mem_alloc or thread_dispatch, and it goes down the fault path to panic.

    Q53Why is stval 0 on the faculty VM but 0x14102ff3 in your sandbox?

    For an illegal instruction, the specification lets the hardware report either the instruction bits or zero in stval. Newer QEMU reports the bits; the VM's QEMU evidently reports zero. The kernel prints whatever it finds, so both are correct. scause = 2 is what identifies the fault.

    Q54The trap frame's layout is written twice, in C++ and in assembly. How do you keep them consistent?

    h/trap_frame.hpp has static_asserts for the frame's size and the offsets of ra, t1, a0, a4, t6, sepc and sstatus, using the same numbers as the assembly literals. Adding or removing a field, or moving one of those seven, breaks the build. A swap between unpinned fields, or a change to the assembly, is not caught by anything, so the rule is to change both together and re-run public test 1.

    Drill

    Drill 2Skip an illegal instruction instead of killing the thread

    Task. "When a user thread executes an illegal instruction, print the report as now, but let the thread continue after that instruction." This is a question about sepc: which instruction does sret return to after a fault, and how do you move past it?

    Where: src/trap.cpp, handleFault (trap.cpp:40–54). Only the user-mode branch changes. The supervisor-mode branch keeps panicking.

    Why it works: sepc in the frame points at the faulting instruction, exactly as it pointed at the ecall for a system call. Adding 4 skips it, and every instruction is 4 bytes long because the build has no compressed instructions. return goes back through trapHandler to trapEntry, which restores the frame and executes sret.

    Watch out for: writing Riscv::w_sepc(Riscv::r_sepc() + 4). It compiles, and it does nothing, because trapEntry reloads sepc from the frame. Skipping any fault other than an illegal instruction would be wrong: a bad load would just leave its destination register with a stale value.

    Test. Public test 7 itself:
