    Run in the sandbox: after B: i=10 the report ends with "raised in user mode - the instruction is skipped", B carries on (B: i=11 … B: i=15, B finished!), the test prints Test se nije uspesno zavrsio and TEST 7 (...), and QEMU exits by itself, a regular termination. From the test's point of view, the kernel now fails test 7. That shows why the unmodified kernel kills the thread. The own test suite still passes on the patched kernel.

    start="7">
  • The system call dispatcher
    • <

    trapHandler has recognised an ecall from user mode and advanced sepc. What remains is to find out which call it is, take its arguments, do the work, and put the result where trapEntry will load it into a0. That is Syscalls::dispatch: one switch over the code, with the argument checking done in small helpers above it.

    h/syscalls.hpp

    h/syscalls.hpp28 lines · in the submission zip as inc/syscalls.hpp

    The rule in the class comment is the most important one in this chapter. Arguments are read from the saved frame, and the result is written into the saved frame. The live registers are only scratch. A system call such as THREAD_DISPATCH or a blocking SEM_WAIT switches to other threads half way through. When it resumes, the processor's registers hold whatever the kernel happened to leave in them. The trap frame on this thread's own stack is the only record of this thread's user registers, and trapEntry's epilogue loads a0 from it.

    src/syscalls.cpp: the helpers

    src/syscalls.cpp193 lines · in the submission zip as src/syscalls.cpp

    asResult turns an int code into a 64-bit register value. Casting to long first sign-extends it, so −3 becomes 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFD. The C API's (int) cast then gives −3 back. Casting the int straight to uint64 would also sign-extend, since conversion goes through the value. Going through long states the intent.

    thread_create and sem_open hand the kernel a pointer to a handle: the kernel writes the new handle through it. A null, misaligned or out-of-memory pointer would make that store fault in supervisor mode, which is a kernel panic. So before writing, the kernel checks three things: the address is aligned for the type, it is at or above the start of RAM (0x80000000), and the whole object ends before HEAP_END_ADDR, the end of RAM. The last test is written as address <= end - size rather than address + size <= end, so that a huge address cannot wrap around to a small sum.

    What this protects against, and what not. It turns mistakes (a null pointer, a garbage value) into SYS_ERR_BAD_ARGUMENT instead of a kernel crash. It does not defend against malice: hw.lib's memory protection lets user code write anywhere in RAM directly, kernel data included, so a hostile program needs no system call to corrupt the kernel. The checks are sized to what this platform can actually enforce.

    The handle pointer is checked here, at the boundary. The rest is checked inside _thread::create (chapter 8): a null body, and a stack that must be a live 4096-byte allocation. The body pointer is not checked for being a valid function, and it does not need to be for the kernel's sake. The kernel never calls the body: threadWrapper does, in user mode. So a wild body pointer can never make the kernel fault. The worst case runs in user mode: it jumps to whatever bytes are there (PMP lets user mode execute all of memory), and either faults, which kills only that thread, or does damage first, which user code can do deliberately anyway.

    Every semaphore call starts the same way: turn the raw a1 into a semaphore through _sem::fromHandle, which returns nullptr for anything that is not an open semaphore (chapter 9 explains how that is decided safely). SEM_WAIT and SEM_WAIT_N share semWait, and SEM_SIGNAL and SEM_SIGNAL_N share semSignal. The plain calls pass n = 1.

    The console helpers, lines 85–104, are covered in chapter 10.

    Syscalls::dispatch: one case per code

    MEM_ALLOC's result is a pointer, or 0 for failure. It goes into a0 as it is, without asResult, because it is not an error code. The count in a1 is already in blocks: the C API did the rounding.

    • THREAD_EXIT does not come back for a user thread: _thread::exit() switches away for good. The line that stores its result runs only if the exit was refused, which happens only for the main thread, and the main thread never makes system calls. The line is kept so that every path, even one that cannot happen, leaves a defined a0.
    • THREAD_DISPATCH calls _thread::dispatch() and continues when this thread is scheduled again, after other threads have run on their own stacks. frame is a reference to this thread's own trap frame, on this thread's own stack, and that stack has been left alone in the meantime. So the reference is still valid when the call continues. The result is SYS_OK, because a void call still leaves a defined value in a0.

    SEM_WAIT_N and SEM_SIGNAL_N take n from a2, cast from the 64-bit register to the C API's unsigned.

    TIME_SLEEP needs a timer that interrupts, which is zadatak 4, so it answers SYS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED. The function still exists so that code calling it, such as Thread::sleep and PeriodicThread, compiles and gets an error back instead of the default case's generic one.

    An unknown code is an error returned to the caller, SYS_ERR_GENERIC, never a kernel fault.

    Why a switch and not a table of function pointers? Each case is one line of real work with its own way of reading arguments and writing the result (a pointer for MEM_ALLOC, a byte for GETC, asResult for the rest). A table would need a common signature and an adapter per call, which puts the same lines somewhere less visible. Speed is not a concern either way: the switch costs a few instructions. The helpers above the switch follow the order of the ABI enum (memory, threads, semaphores, time, console), so you can scan both in parallel.

    Questions

    Q55Why does the dispatcher read arguments from the trap frame and not from a1–a4 directly?

    By the time C++ code runs, the registers have been used by trapHandler and the dispatcher, and after any context switch they hold another thread's leftovers. The trap frame on this thread's stack is the one authoritative copy of this thread's user registers. The result goes into the frame's a0 for the same reason: that is what trapEntry loads into a0 before sret.

    Q56After _thread::dispatch() returns inside the THREAD_DISPATCH case, much later, is frame still valid?

    Yes. It refers to this thread's own trap frame, on this thread's own stack. While the thread was switched out, nothing touched that stack. The other threads ran on their own stacks. When the thread is resumed, it is back on its stack with its frame intact.

    Q57What does isInRam check, and why is it needed?

    That a pointer the kernel is about to write a handle through is aligned and lies entirely inside RAM, [0x80000000, HEAP_END_ADDR). A bad pointer would otherwise fault inside the kernel, which panics the whole system. With the check, the caller gets SYS_ERR_BAD_ARGUMENT. It catches mistakes, not malice: user code can write kernel memory directly anyway.

    Q58Why is the body pointer of thread_create not validated the same way?

    Only a null body is refused. The kernel never calls the body: threadWrapper does, in user mode. So a garbage body can never make the kernel fault. At worst it runs garbage in user mode until it faults, and the fault path ends that thread.

    Q59What happens if user code issues an ecall with an unknown code?

    The default case sets a0 to SYS_ERR_GENERIC, and the call returns normally.

    Q60Why doesn't MEM_ALLOC's result go through asResult?

    It is a pointer, not an error code: the payload address or 0 (nullptr) on failure. asResult exists to sign-extend negative int codes.

    Q61Walk through everything you would change to add a new system call.

    Five places, top to bottom: a new code in abi::Syscall (h/abi.hpp); the declaration in h/syscall_c.h; the C API function in src/syscall_c.cpp, which is one __syscall with the arguments in order; the kernel function that does the work, in the class that owns the data; and a case in Syscalls::dispatch that reads the arguments from frame.a1…, calls the kernel function and writes frame.a0. Optionally, a C++ wrapper. The drill below does exactly this.

    Q62What does a void system call such as thread_dispatch leave in a0?

    SYS_OK (0). Every system call writes a0, so the register's value after the call is always defined. The rule is: nothing but a0 changes.

    Drill

    Drill 3Add a system call: how much memory is free?

    Task. "Add size_t mem_get_free_space(), code 0x03. It returns how many bytes could still be allocated." This is the standard "add a system call" modification, and the pattern is always the same five places. The kernel-side work lives with the data it reads: the free list is MemoryAllocator's, so the counting function goes there.

    Where:

    1. h/abi.hpp: the code, MEM_GET_FREE_SPACE = 0x03, in the enum.
    2. h/syscall_c.h: the declaration.
    3. src/syscall_c.cpp: the C API function, one __syscall.
    4. h/memory_allocator.hpp, src/memory_allocator.cpp: MemoryAllocator::freeBytes(), a walk over the free list adding up each segment's payload.
    5. src/syscalls.cpp: the case, which writes the result into frame.a0.

    Watch out for:

    • Counting the header blocks as free space. A free segment of b blocks can hand out at most b − 1 of them.
    • Wrapping the result in asResult. It is a size, not an error code, so it goes into a0 as it is.
    • Using a new code that clashes with an existing one. The examiner usually names the code. If not, the next free number in the group is the natural choice.

    Test. Read the free space, allocate 1000 bytes, read again, free, read again:

    The test program used: put it in test/userMain.cpp of a scratch copy of the project, in place of the public tests' userMain
    #include "../h/syscall_c.h"

namespace
{
void print(const char *text) { while (*text != '\0') { putc(*text++); } }

void printNumber(uint64 n)
{
    char digits[20];
    int count = 0;
    do { digits[count++] = (char) ('0' + n % 10); n /= 10; } while (n != 0);
    while (count > 0) { putc(digits[--count]); }
}

void report(const char *label, size_t value)
{
    print(label); printNumber(value); putc('\n');
}
}

void userMain()
{
    const size_t before = mem_get_free_space();
    report("free before:        ", before);

    void *p = mem_alloc(1000);          /* 16 blocks + 1 header block */
    const size_t during = mem_get_free_space();
    report("free after 1000 B:  ", during);
    report("difference:         ", before - during);

    mem_free(p);
    const size_t after = mem_get_free_space();
    report("free after mem_free:", after);
    print(after == before ? "coalesced back: yes\n" : "coalesced back: NO\n");
}

    Run in the sandbox (GCC 9.4): free before: 134176768, free after 1000 B: 134175680, difference: 1088, free after mem_free: 134176768, coalesced back: yes. The absolute numbers depend on the size of the kernel image, since the heap starts right after it, and will differ on your build. The difference of 1088 and the return to the starting value will not. 1000 bytes are 16 blocks, plus a header block makes 17, and 17 × 64 = 1088. Freeing merges the segment back with its neighbour, so the total returns exactly. The build's own t0–t6 check on the C API stayed clean, and the own test suite still passes (84 of 84).

    start="8">
  • Threads: control blocks, the switch, the ready queue
    • <

    This chapter covers zadatak 2: creating a thread, switching between threads, and ending one. Five files take part. tcb.hpp/tcb.cpp hold _thread, the thread control block and every state change. asm_routines.cpp holds yield, the switch itself, and threadStart, a new thread's way into user mode. thread_queue and scheduler hold the ready queue.

    thread_create creates and starts a thread over start_routine(arg) and writes its handle. thread_exit ends the calling thread. thread_dispatch "potencijalno oduzima procesor tekućoj i daje nekoj drugoj (ili istoj) niti": it may take the processor from the current thread and give it to another one, or to the same one. Zadatak 2 is graded as synchronous context switching: switches happen only when a thread asks for one.

    The four states

    h/tcb.hpp: the control block

    h/tcb.hpp144 lines · in the submission zip as inc/tcb.hpp

    Three ideas from this comment carry the whole chapter:

    • _thread is the handle. A thread_t is a _thread *, with no cast and no table in between.
    • Registers live on the stack, not in the control block. A thread that is not running has two frames on its stack: the trap frame from its last system call (its user registers) and, below it, the yield frame from the moment it gave up the processor (the kernel's registers). The control block stores one number: sp, which leads to both.
    • No locks. Interrupts are never enabled, so exactly one flow of control is ever inside the kernel.

    block and unblock are how _sem (chapter 9) makes a thread wait without ever touching _thread's fields. The semaphore owns the queue and decides when to release; _thread owns the state and decides how. The result of the wait travels through the waiting thread's own control block, because by the time it runs again the semaphore may have been destroyed.

    The constructors are private. Only adoptBootContext and create can make a thread, so every thread goes through the checks in create and the bookkeeping that goes with them. ThreadQueue is a friend because it links threads through their next field (below). operator new and operator delete redirect new _thread and delete to slot storage (chapter 4), and noexcept makes new return nullptr on exhaustion instead of constructing at address 0.

    A control block is 40 bytes: sp, next, stack, state, wanted, waitResult. The four static members are the kernel's thread bookkeeping: who is running, who the main thread is, which finished thread still waits to be freed, and how many user threads are alive.

    src/tcb.cpp

    src/tcb.cpp178 lines · in the submission zip as src/tcb.cpp

    The static members are initialised with constants. Nothing here needs code to run at start-up, which matters because nothing would run it.

    Two constructors

    The boot context is already running, so it starts RUNNING, with sp = 0 until its first switch saves a real value. stack = nullptr says "not ours to free": the main thread runs on hw.lib's stack0.

    This constructor is how a thread that has never run can be switched to in exactly the same way as one that has. yield always restores a YieldFrame from the new thread's stack and returns to the ra in it. So the constructor writes one at the top of the new stack, as if the thread had called yield() there:

    • Line 38: the top is stack + 4096, rounded down to a multiple of 16 as the RISC-V ABI requires for sp. mem_alloc returns 64-aligned memory, so the rounding changes nothing in practice. It is there so the alignment does not depend on that.
    • Line 42 zeroes the frame with a loop, not memset. There is no C library, and a struct assignment of that size could make the compiler emit a call to memset that would fail to link.
    • Lines 44–46: ra is where yield's ret goes, which is threadStart. s1 and s2 carry the body and argument. They are callee-saved registers, so yield restores them from this frame.
    • Line 48: sp points at the frame, exactly where a real yield would have left it.

    Storage, and the main thread

    Deleting a thread frees its stack as well. From a successful thread_create on, the kernel owns that block.

    create()

    Every check comes before any change (lines 83–88). A refused call leaves nothing behind: no half-built thread, no changed count, and the stack block still belongs to the caller, who frees it (chapter 5). The stack check matters because the constructor is about to write 112 bytes into that block. isAllocated(stack, 4096) confirms that stackTop − 4096 is the start of a live allocation with room for a whole stack (chapter 4).

    After that: the handle is written, the thread is counted, and it joins the back of the ready queue. The creator keeps running; the new thread runs when its turn comes. The handle is written before the new thread can possibly run, so a thread may read its own handle through its argument.

    exit()

    A finished thread is marked FINISHED and uncounted, then dispatch() switches away. It never comes back, because dispatch() puts only RUNNING threads back in the ready queue. The main thread is refused because it is the thread that halts the system. It also cannot reach this code, since it never makes a system call, so the check is defensive.

    dispatch(): the only place a switch is decided

    Every context switch in this kernel goes through these lines. They are reached from THREAD_DISPATCH, from a sem_wait that blocks, from GETC/PUTC waiting for the UART, from exit() (a system call or a fault), and from the main thread's idle loop.

    1. Line 110: release the previous zombie (below).
    2. Lines 112–122: decide what happens to the thread giving up the processor, according to its state: - RUNNING: it is merely yielding. It becomes READY and goes to the back of the ready queue. - FINISHED: it just exited. It cannot be freed yet (below), so it is parked as the zombie. - BLOCKED: block() has already put it in a semaphore's queue. Nothing to do here.
    3. Line 124: take the next thread from the front of the ready queue. The queue is never empty here. While a user thread runs, the main thread is READY in the queue, and when the main thread is the one calling, it has just put itself in. The panic is a guard against a kernel bug.
    4. Line 128: switch, unless the next thread is the same one. In this kernel that never actually happens. While a user thread runs, the main thread is READY in the queue, and the main thread dispatches only after checking that the queue is not empty. So the queue always yields a different thread. The guard matters once the idle drill below takes the main thread out of the queue.

    The switch itself: yield

    The declarations and the frame layout are in asm_routines.hpp:

    yield saves only ra and s0–s11. It is called like any C++ function from dispatch(), so the compiler has already dealt with the caller-saved registers (a0–a7, t0–t6): whatever dispatch() still needs of them, it saved in its own frame, and the rest are dead by the calling convention. The user's values of those registers are safe in the trap frame higher up the same stack. So the YieldFrame holds the kernel's state, and the TrapFrame holds the user's.

    yield takes the addresses of the two saved stack pointers, &old->sp and &running->sp, not the threads. The assembly therefore knows nothing about _thread's layout, and there is no field offset to keep in sync with it.

    The final ret is the whole trick. It is executed on the new stack, with the ra restored from that stack. There are only two places that can be: back inside the new thread's own earlier call to yield(), so dispatch() returns in that thread, which then returns from its system call (or, for the main thread, into its loop), or threadStart, for a thread that has never run.

    A new thread's first steps: threadStart

    threadStart runs in supervisor mode, on the new thread's stack, with sp already at the top because yield popped the fabricated frame. It does four things:

    1. a0 ← s1 (body) and a1 ← s2 (arg), the two arguments of threadWrapper(body, arg);
    2. sepc ← the address of threadWrapper, computed with lla: PC-relative, never through a global offset table;
    3. clear SPP in sstatus, so that sret goes to user mode. SPP is bit 8, and csrci's immediate has only 5 bits (bits 0–4), so the mask goes through t0. Using t0 is safe because the new thread has no user registers yet;
    4. sret: user mode, pc = threadWrapper.

    A new thread has no trap frame when it starts. It enters user mode directly, and its first frame is pushed at its first ecall. This is the only place in the kernel where user mode is entered other than returning from a trap. Public test 7 proves it works: code started this way cannot read sepc.

    The zombie, and why a thread cannot free itself

    The count covers threads made by create() that have not called exit(). A zombie is no longer counted, and the main thread never was.

    When a thread exits, the processor is still standing on its stack: exit(), dispatch() and the system call's frames all live there. yield will also write the old sp into its control block on the way out. So the thread cannot be freed inside its own last dispatch(). It is parked in zombie, and the next dispatch() frees it. That call necessarily runs on a different stack, because a zombie is never scheduled again. delete zombie returns the control block to its slot, and ~_thread returns the stack to the heap. At most one zombie exists at a time: every dispatch() releases the old one before it can create a new one.

    Measured in the sandbox with an instrumented build (which paints every stack at creation and checks how much was overwritten when it is freed): over public tests 1 and 2 the heap ends exactly one stack short, 65 blocks, which is the last zombie still parked when the system halts. The own tests create 40,000 threads one after another. All succeed, although the heap could hold only about 32,000 stacks at once, so released threads are really freed.

    Blocking and unblocking

    block() records the request, marks the thread BLOCKED, appends it to the given queue, and dispatches. Because the thread is BLOCKED, dispatch() leaves it where it is: not in the ready queue. When someone calls unblock(result) on it, it becomes READY and joins the back of the ready queue. When it next runs, dispatch() returns inside block(), which returns the result stored in the thread's own control block. It deliberately reads nothing else: the queue it waited in belonged to a semaphore that may no longer exist.

    unblock panics on a thread that is not BLOCKED. A READY thread is already in the ready queue, and putting it in a second time would overwrite its next link and corrupt the queue. That is a kernel bug and should stop the system loudly.

    kernel::ThreadQueue: a queue linked through the threads

    h/thread_queue.hpp42 lines · in the submission zip as inc/thread_queue.hpp
    src/thread_queue.cpp28 lines · in the submission zip as src/thread_queue.cpp

    The queue is intrusive: the link is a field of the thread itself (_thread::next), not a separately allocated node. Putting a thread in a queue therefore never allocates and cannot fail, and put and get are O(1) with a head and a tail pointer. The price is that a thread can be in only one queue at a time. The states guarantee that anyway.

    The constructor is constexpr, which matters for the one queue that is a global object: Scheduler::ready. A global whose constructor is constexpr is set up by the compiler as constant data. With an ordinary constructor it would need a dynamic initialiser at start-up, which nothing runs in this kernel. The queue would then stay as whatever the zeroed memory holds. Here that happens to be the right value, but only by accident.

    get clears the removed thread's next (line 24), so no stale link ever survives outside a queue.

    kernel::Scheduler: the ready queue

    h/scheduler.hpp38 lines · in the submission zip as inc/scheduler.hpp
    src/scheduler.cpp23 lines · in the submission zip as src/scheduler.cpp

    First come, first served: the thread that became ready first runs first. The assignment says that is enough. It is also the easiest policy to reason about in a cooperative kernel, where a thread keeps the processor until it gives it away. All policy lives in put and get, so a different policy changes this class and nothing else. isEmpty exists for the deadlock check in System::run.

    Stack usage, measured with the instrumented build on public tests 1–4 and the own tests: the deepest any thread went was 904 of its 4096 bytes (public test 2). Threads blocked on a semaphore, with user frames, a trap frame, the kernel's frames and a yield frame all on one stack, stayed under 750. The PDF prefers a separate kernel stack as safer against user stack overflow. Running the kernel on the thread's stack is the simplest variant it describes, and the measurements show the 4096 bytes are ample for these programs.

    Questions

    Q63What does your thread control block contain, and where are a thread's registers saved?

    sp, the queue link next, the stack block's address, the state, and two fields used while blocked (wanted, waitResult): 40 bytes. The registers are on the thread's own stack: user registers in the trap frame from its last system call, kernel callee-saved registers in the yield frame from its last switch. sp leads to both.

    Q64Why does yield take &old->sp and &new->sp instead of the two threads?

    So the assembly never needs to know where sp sits inside _thread. With yield(_thread *, _thread *) the assembly would load at a hard-coded offset, and that offset would have to be kept in sync with the class by hand or by a static_assert. Passing the two addresses removes the question.

    Q65Why does yield save only ra and s0–s11?

    yield is called like a normal function from dispatch(). Under the calling convention, the caller-saved registers (a, t) may be destroyed by any call, so dispatch() does not rely on them surviving. Only the callee-saved registers and the return address must look unchanged when yield "returns", possibly on another thread. The user's values of every register are already in the trap frame higher up the same stack.

    Q66How does a thread that has never run get started by the same yield that resumes old threads?

    Its constructor fabricates a YieldFrame at the top of its stack, with ra = threadStart, s1 = body, s2 = arg, and points sp at it. The first yield to it pops that frame and "returns" into threadStart, which moves s1, s2 into a0, a1, sets sepc = threadWrapper, clears SPP, and executes sret into user mode.

    Q67Why s1 and s2 for the body and argument?

    They must be registers that yield restores from the frame, which means callee-saved ones. Any s register would work. s0 doubles as the frame pointer in this build (-fno-omit-frame-pointer), so s1 and s2 are the natural first choice.

    Q68Why does threadStart use li t0, 0x100 and csrc instead of csrci?

    csrci takes a 5-bit immediate, which can only name bits 0–4. SPP is bit 8, so the mask must come from a register.

    Q69Why lla and not la in threadStart?

    la may load the address through the global offset table, depending on how the code is compiled. lla always computes it PC-relatively with auipc + addi. In a naked function with basic asm, lla is the form that never depends on the GOT.

    Q70What happens to a thread's memory when it finishes, and when?

    It becomes FINISHED and is parked as _thread::zombie. The next dispatch(), by whichever thread, deletes it. That returns the control block to its slot, and the destructor returns the 4096-byte stack to the heap.

    Q71Why can't a finishing thread free its own stack in exit()?

    It is standing on that stack: exit() and dispatch() run on it, and yield still writes the old sp into the control block. Freeing it first would mean running on, and writing into, memory the allocator considers free. The next dispatch runs on a different stack, so it can do it safely.

    Q72Can there be more than one zombie at once?

    No. Every dispatch() releases the existing zombie at its start, before it can park a new one at its end.

    Q73Where is the main thread's stack, and is it ever freed?

    It is hw.lib's boot stack stack0. adoptBootContext gives the main thread stack = nullptr, so the destructor would free nothing. The main thread never finishes anyway.

    Q74Is the main thread in the ready queue?

    Whenever a user thread is running, yes: it is READY and takes its turn like everyone else. When it gets the processor it checks the live-thread count, possibly panics on a deadlock, and dispatches again. The drill below changes that.

    Q75Can the ready queue be empty when dispatch() takes the next thread?

    Not without a kernel bug. If a user thread is running, the main thread is READY in the queue. If the main thread is running, it has just put itself in. The panic on line 125 guards against a bug.

    Q76What is the difference between a READY and a BLOCKED thread? Who wakes a BLOCKED one?

    A READY thread is in the ready queue and will run in its turn. A BLOCKED thread is in exactly one semaphore's queue and will not run until that semaphore's signal or close calls unblock() on it, which makes it READY again.

    Q77Why does unblock() panic if the thread is not BLOCKED?

    A thread that is not BLOCKED is either RUNNING or already in the ready queue. Putting it in the ready queue again would overwrite its next link and corrupt the queue. That can only be a kernel bug, so it stops the system loudly.

    Q78Why is ThreadQueue intrusive, and what does that cost?

    The link is inside _thread, so queueing never allocates, never fails, and is O(1). The cost is that a thread can be in only one queue at a time. The states guarantee that: READY means in the ready queue, BLOCKED means in one semaphore's queue, and RUNNING or FINISHED means in none.

    Q79Why is ThreadQueue's constructor constexpr?

    Scheduler::ready is a global ThreadQueue. With a constexpr constructor, the compiler initialises it as constant data. Otherwise it would need a dynamic initialiser, and this kernel's image has no .init_array and nothing that would run one.

    Q80How would you add priorities to the scheduler?

    Give _thread a priority field, set when it is created. Make Scheduler hold one ThreadQueue per priority level. put appends to the thread's level, and get takes from the highest non-empty level. Nothing outside Scheduler, _thread's constructor, and the API that sets the priority would change. A starvation guard, such as ageing, would be the natural follow-up question.

    Q81How much of a 4096-byte stack is used, and what happens on overflow?

    Measured: at most 904 bytes (public test 2), and under 750 for threads blocked on a semaphore. Nothing detects an overflow. The first thing an overflowing stack overwrites is its own segment header, the block just below the stack. When the thread is later freed, freeBlocks then fails the magic check, and ~_thread ignores the error, so the stack silently leaks. Further down, it corrupts the segment below it in the heap. This is the risk the PDF points out when it prefers a separate kernel stack.

    Drills

    Drill 4A system call that returns the running thread's ID

    Task. "Add int thread_get_id(), code 0x14. The main thread has ID 0, and user threads are numbered 1, 2, 3 … in creation order." This is the add-a-system-call pattern from chapter 7, plus one field in the control block.

    Where: the four boundary places (h/abi.hpp, h/syscall_c.h, src/syscall_c.cpp, src/syscalls.cpp). In _thread: a field id, a static counter lastId, and a static accessor runningId(). The constructors set the ID: 0 for the boot context, ++lastId for a new thread.

    Watch out for:

    • The order in the member-initialiser lists. id is declared last, so it must come last in the list. -Wall includes -Wreorder, -Werror turns it into an error, and the build stops.
    • The static counter's initialiser must be a constant. int _thread::lastId = 0; is. Anything computed at start-up would never run.
    • The ID is read from running. The system call executes in the calling thread's own context, so "the running thread" is the caller.
    The test program used: put it in test/userMain.cpp of a scratch copy of the project, in place of the public tests' userMain
    #include "../h/syscall_c.h"

namespace
{
void print(const char *text) { while (*text != '\0') { putc(*text++); } }

volatile int finished = 0;

void worker(void *name)
{
    print((const char *) name);
    print(": id ");
    putc((char) ('0' + thread_get_id()));
    putc('\n');
    finished++;
}
}

void userMain()
{
    print("userMain: id ");
    putc((char) ('0' + thread_get_id()));
    putc('\n');

    thread_t a, b;
    thread_create(&a, worker, (void *) "worker A");
    thread_create(&b, worker, (void *) "worker B");
    while (finished < 2) { thread_dispatch(); }
}

    Run in the sandbox: userMain: id 1, worker A: id 2, worker B: id 3, then a regular termination. The own suite still passes (84 of 84), and sizeof(_thread) stays 40 because the new field fills the padding at the end of the struct.

    Drill 5thread_join: wait until another thread has finished

    Task. "Add int thread_join(thread_t handle): the caller blocks until that thread has finished. Joining a thread that has already finished returns at once." This is the most likely larger modification, and the tricky part is not the waiting. It is the handle: a finished thread's control block is freed at the next dispatch, so the handle may point at a free slot, or even at a newer thread in the same slot.

    The design.

    • Each thread gets a queue of joiners: threads blocked until it finishes. Waiting is block(thread->joiners, 0), the same mechanism a semaphore uses.
    • exit() releases every joiner with unblock(SYS_OK) before it switches away.
    • The handle is checked the way chapter 9 checks semaphore handles. First SlotAllocator<_thread>::owns(handle), which compares addresses only. Then a magic word placed first in _thread: freeing a slot overwrites the first word with the free-list link, so a released thread no longer shows the magic. A slot without the magic held a thread that finished and was released, so the call returns SYS_OK.
    • A thread that has finished but not yet been released still has its magic. It is the zombie until the next dispatch. So join must also test state == FINISHED and return at once. Without that test, a joiner would block on the zombie's joiners queue, and the very next dispatch would free that queue with the joiner still in it: the joiner would never be released.
    • Joining yourself would block for ever, so it is refused.

    Where: the four boundary places (code 0x15); h/tcb.hpp (the join declaration, magic, joiners, and #include "thread_queue.hpp", since a member of type ThreadQueue needs the full class); src/tcb.cpp (the constructors, exit, join).

    Watch out for:

    • magic must be the first field, because that is the word the slot allocator overwrites. Anywhere else, a freed thread would still look alive.
    • Do not rely on the destructor to clear the magic. GCC 9.4 removes a store to an object whose lifetime is ending (chapter 9 explains this for _sem).
    • Release the joiners in exit() before dispatch(). After it, the thread never runs again.
    • A handle whose slot has been reused names the new thread, and a join then waits for that one. The FIFO slot list delays reuse for as long as possible, but with a bare pointer as the handle, nothing can prevent it completely.
    • Two edge cases this patch leaves as they are: a thread slot that never held a thread also answers SYS_OK (it has no magic either), and joining the main thread's slot is not refused, so it blocks until the deadlock check fires. Neither can happen with a handle thread_create returned.
    The test program used: put it in test/userMain.cpp of a scratch copy of the project, in place of the public tests' userMain
    #include "../h/syscall_c.h"

namespace
{
void print(const char *text) { while (*text != '\0') { putc(*text++); } }

volatile bool workerDone = false;

void worker(void *)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { print("worker: step\n"); thread_dispatch(); }
    print("worker: done\n");
    workerDone = true;
}

void selfJoiner(void *self)
{
    const int result = thread_join(*(thread_t *) self);
    print(result == SYS_ERR_BAD_ARGUMENT ? "self: joining itself is refused\n" : "self: WRONG result\n");
}
}

void userMain()
{
    thread_t w;
    thread_create(&w, worker, nullptr);
    print("main: joining the worker\n");
    const int first = thread_join(w);
    print(first == 0 && workerDone ? "main: join returned after the worker finished\n"
                                   : "main: WRONG - join returned early\n");

    print(thread_join(w) == 0 ? "main: a second join returns at once\n" : "main: WRONG second join\n");

    int notAThread = 0;
    print(thread_join((thread_t) &notAThread) == SYS_ERR_BAD_HANDLE ? "main: a non-thread handle is refused\n"
                                                                    : "main: WRONG non-thread result\n");

    thread_t s;
    thread_create(&s, selfJoiner, &s);
    thread_join(s);
    print("main: done\n");
}

    Run in the sandbox: the worker's three steps and "worker: done" print before "main: join returned after the worker finished". A second join returns at once. A handle that is not a thread slot gets SYS_ERR_BAD_HANDLE, and a thread joining itself gets SYS_ERR_BAD_ARGUMENT. The system terminates regularly, and the own suite still passes (84 of 84).

    Drill 6The main thread runs only when nothing else is ready

    Task. "Your idle thread takes a turn every round. Make it run only when no other thread is ready, as the PDF suggests." Only _thread::dispatch changes: the main thread never goes into the ready queue, and when the queue is empty, it is the one that runs.

    Why the rest still works. System::run's loop is unchanged. The main thread now gets the processor only when the ready queue is empty. That happens either because every user thread has finished (count 0: the loop ends and the system halts) or because the last runnable thread just blocked or exited while others are still alive, all of them BLOCKED (the deadlock panic, as before). A thread that dispatches with nobody else ready simply continues, without a pointless round trip through the main thread.

    Watch out for: the old panic for an empty queue must go. An empty queue now means "run the main thread". Invariant 12 in chapter 13 changes as well: the main thread is READY without being in any queue.

    Run in the sandbox on the patched kernel: public test 1 ends with a regular termination, the deliberate deadlock still ends in "every user thread is blocked on a semaphore - deadlock", and the own suite passes (84 of 84).

    Drill 7Time slicing: preempt a thread that never yields

    Task. "Add time slicing: a thread that runs for DEFAULT_TIME_SLICE timer ticks without giving up the processor is switched out." This is the heart of zadatak 4, the asynchronous context switch, without time_sleep and the console interrupts. It shows how much of the design is already in place: the trap saves the complete state, including sepc and sstatus, so a switch from inside an interrupt is exactly as safe as one from inside a system call.

    Three changes:

    1. System::initialize: keep SSIE enabled (the timer, which hw.lib delivers as a supervisor software interrupt) and mask only STIE and SEIE. Clear sstatus.SIE explicitly as a safeguard. It is already 0 when main starts, every trap clears it again, and the only sret that restores it goes to user mode. So supervisor mode is never interrupted, and the kernel stays one critical section: only user code can be preempted.
    2. trapHandler, in the interrupt branch: acknowledge SSIP as before, count the tick, and every DEFAULT_TIME_SLICE ticks call _thread::dispatch().
    3. A tick counter in trap.cpp, with a constant initialiser.

    Why nothing else changes. An interrupted thread's frame holds sepc pointing at the interrupted instruction, and it is not advanced, so the thread resumes exactly where it was when its turn comes. The kernel code never runs with interrupts on, so none of its data structures needs a lock. The main thread's idle loop runs in supervisor mode and is never preempted, which is fine because it dispatches anyway.

    Watch out for:

    • The kernel's safety rests on sstatus.SIE being 0 whenever kernel code runs. On this platform that already holds, and the explicit clear only guards it. Any change that set SIE in supervisor mode would allow interrupts inside the kernel, in the middle of a MemoryAllocator call for example, and then the kernel would need locks.
    • The tick counter is global, not per thread. A thread that starts just after a voluntary switch may get a shorter first slice. A per-thread counter reset in dispatch() would fix that.
    • With preemption, test outputs interleave differently. Public test 1's ordering becomes timing-dependent, which is still correct behaviour.
    The test program used: put it in test/userMain.cpp of a scratch copy of the project, in place of the public tests' userMain
    #include "../h/syscall_c.h"

namespace
{
void print(const char *text) { while (*text != '\0') { putc(*text++); } }

volatile int finished = 0;

/* Never calls thread_dispatch: without preemption it keeps the processor
   until it is done. */
void spinner(void *name)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    {
        for (volatile uint64 k = 0; k < 20000000; k++) {}
        print((const char *) name);
        putc((char) ('0' + i));
        putc('\n');
    }
    finished++;
}
}

void userMain()
{
    thread_t a, b;
    thread_create(&a, spinner, (void *) "A step ");
    thread_create(&b, spinner, (void *) "B step ");
    while (finished < 2) { thread_dispatch(); }
    print("both done\n");
}

    Run in the sandbox with two threads that spin without ever calling thread_dispatch. Unmodified kernel: A step 0 … A step 4, then B step 0 … B step 4, because A never gives the processor away. Patched kernel, one run: A step 0, B step 0, B step 1, B step 2, A step 1, A step 2, A step 3, B step 3, B step 4, A step 4. The exact interleaving changes from run to run, because it depends on when the timer fires. It interleaves every time. Public tests 1 and 3 still end with a regular termination on the patched kernel, and the own suite passes (84 of 84).

    start="9">
  • Semaphores (zadatak 3)
    • <

    A semaphore here is a count of available units plus a queue of threads waiting for more units than there are. The design questions are all about the edges. What does wait_n do when a request is larger than one unit? Whom does signal_n release? What happens to waiters when the semaphore is closed under them? And how does the kernel tell a real semaphore handle from garbage without faulting?

    sem_close: "Sve niti koje su se zatekle da čekaju na semaforu se deblokiraju, pri čemu njihov wait vraća grešku": every waiting thread is released, and its wait returns an error. sem_wait_n: "Ukoliko je trenutna vrednost semafora veća ili jednaka n, vrednost se umanjuje za n i funkcija se odmah uspešno završava. U suprotnom, pozivajuća nit se blokira dok ne postane moguće izvršiti operaciju (ili dok semafor ne bude dealociran)." sem_signal_n increases the value by n, and "može doći do deblokiranja jedne ili više niti". How any of this is implemented is left to us.

    h/ksemaphore.hpp

    h/ksemaphore.hpp96 lines · in the submission zip as inc/ksemaphore.hpp

    The textbook semaphore from the lectures, if (--value < 0) block();, uses a negative value to count waiters. That works because every waiter wants exactly one unit. With wait_n, one waiter may want 5 and another 2, and a single negative number cannot say who still needs how much. So here value is always the number of units available now, never negative, and each blocked thread remembers its own request in its control block (_thread::wanted). For requests of one unit the behaviour is exactly the classic semaphore.

    open and close are static, and they are the only way to create or destroy a semaphore. close destroys the object, so it cannot sensibly be a member function called on that object. fromHandle is how the dispatcher turns a raw user value into a semaphore, or refuses it.

    The constructor and destructor are private: nobody can delete a semaphore without going through close, which releases its waiters first. Storage comes from SlotAllocator<_sem> (chapter 4), 32 bytes per semaphore.

    magic is the first field on purpose. When a semaphore is destroyed, the slot allocator writes its free-list link into the slot's first word: a null pointer or the address of another slot, never MAGIC_OPEN. So a closed semaphore's slot can never pass for an open one, and no code in the destructor is needed to make that true.

    Why the destructor does not clear the magic word itself. It would look natural to write magic = 0 in ~_sem. GCC 9.4 deletes that store. The object's lifetime ends right after the destructor, so the compiler may treat a write to it as dead. This was seen in the disassembly of _sem::close. The slot allocator's write is a different matter: it is the free list's own link, read later when the list is walked, so no compiler may remove it. The kernel's correctness rests on that write instead. The same applies to any object you want to "mark dead" in a live modification: a store in its destructor proves nothing.

    src/ksemaphore.cpp

    src/ksemaphore.cpp111 lines · in the submission zip as src/ksemaphore.cpp

    The handle pointer has already been checked by the dispatcher (isInRam, chapter 7), so writing through it cannot fault.

    close: release everyone, then destroy

    Every waiter is taken out of the queue and released with SYS_ERR_SEM_CLOSED. unblock stores that result in the waiter's control block and puts the waiter at the back of the ready queue. Only then is the semaphore deleted. When a released waiter runs again, its block() returns the stored result. It never looks at the semaphore, which by then no longer exists.

    Alternatives that were rejected. Writing the error into the waiter's saved trap frame (frame.a0) would tie the semaphore to the trap layout and bypass the call chain the waiter is suspended in. Letting the waiter check the semaphore after waking would read freed memory: a use after free. The result travels in the waiter's own control block, which is guaranteed to still exist.

    fromHandle: telling a semaphore from anything else

    A handle is whatever 64-bit number the user put in a1. It can be null, misaligned, a wild pointer, a pointer to a closed semaphore, or a pointer to a copy of a semaphore that user code made in its own memory. Two tests, in this order:

    1. Is it the start of one of the kernel's semaphore slots? SlotAllocator<_sem>::owns compares addresses only and reads nothing, so any value at all is safe to ask about. This rejects null, misaligned and wild values, and any forged copy wherever it lies.
    2. Only then is the slot read. It must hold MAGIC_OPEN. A free slot holds a free-list link instead, so a closed semaphore is rejected.

    The first version checked only "aligned, in RAM, and the first word is MAGIC_OPEN". An independent review found two ways past it: a copy of a semaphore made by user code, and the constant MAGIC_OPEN itself, which sits in the kernel image's read-only data. sem_signal on the address of that constant made the kernel follow a wild pointer and panic. Both cases, and a stale handle after new semaphores were opened, are now own tests, and they pass. Run against the old kernel, four of them failed and the constant case panicked it, so the tests do detect what they were written for.

    A closed semaphore's handle stays refused until its slot holds a new semaphore. The FIFO slot list hands a freed slot out only after every other free slot, so a double sem_close or a late sem_signal is still caught after several new sem_opens. Once the slot is reused, the stale handle names the new semaphore, and nothing can tell them apart. sem_t is a bare pointer. The assignment treats the equivalent case for mem_free as undefined behaviour.

    wait

    If value >= n, the units are taken and the call succeeds at once. That is the PDF's "odmah uspešno", and it depends on the value alone, not on whether others are waiting. Otherwise the thread blocks in this semaphore's queue, remembering n. After block() returns, the function does not touch this: close may have deleted the object. The return value comes straight from block(), and it is whatever the releasing thread stored.

    signal

    value grows by n, and then every waiter is offered units in arrival order. Each one whose request fits takes its share and is released. Those that do not fit are moved, in the same order, to a fresh queue, which becomes the semaphore's queue on line 108. That assignment copies two pointers, head and tail: ThreadQueue has no other state. The walk needs no "remove from the middle" operation, only get and put.

    A worked example, the one used in the design notes and the own tests. value is 0, and the queue holds T1 (wants 5), then T2 (wants 2). Then signal_n(3):

    Step Waiter Wants value before Decision value after
    1 T1 5 3 does not fit: stays queued 3
    2 T2 2 3 fits: released with SYS_OK 1

    Afterwards value is 1, T1 still waits, and T2 is at the back of the ready queue. The thread that called signal_n keeps running: nothing in signal or close switches threads. Only a wait that blocks does.

    Why not strict FIFO, where nobody passes the head of the queue? Strict FIFO would leave T2 blocked although 3 units are free, and it would contradict the PDF's rule that a waiter stays blocked only while its operation is impossible. It also would not stop overtaking in general: by the PDF's own rule, a newcomer whose request fits succeeds at once, whatever is queued. The consequence to state at the defence: wait_n promises no fairness, and a large request can be overtaken by a stream of smaller ones. The drill below implements strict FIFO, to show what changes.

    Questions

    Q82How is a semaphore represented in your kernel?

    class _sem, the object sem_t points at. It holds a magic word, value (the units available now, never negative), and a ThreadQueue of blocked threads in arrival order. Storage comes from SlotAllocator<_sem>. Each blocked thread records how many units it wants, and the result its wait will return, in its own control block.

    Q83Why does your value never go negative, unlike the lectures' semaphore?

    With wait_n the waiters want different amounts, and one negative number cannot say who still needs what. So value counts only the available units, and each waiter records its own request. For one-unit requests it behaves exactly like the classic semaphore.

    Q84What does sem_wait do when the value is 0?

    _thread::block(blocked, 1) records the request, marks the running thread BLOCKED, appends it to the semaphore's queue, and calls dispatch(), which switches to the next ready thread without re-queueing this one. The thread runs again only after signal or close has called unblock() on it. block() then returns the stored result, 0 or SYS_ERR_SEM_CLOSED.

    Q85Who runs after a sem_signal that releases a waiter?

    The signalling thread keeps the processor. The released thread becomes READY at the back of the ready queue and runs when its turn comes. Only a blocking wait switches threads inside the semaphore code.

    Q86What happens to threads waiting on a semaphore when it is closed?

    close releases each of them with SYS_ERR_SEM_CLOSED stored in its control block, then deletes the semaphore. Each waiter's sem_wait returns that error, as the PDF requires.

    Q87After waking up, why does a waiter not read anything from the semaphore?

    It may have been woken by close, which then deleted the semaphore. Reading it would be a use after free. The outcome is in the waiter's own control block, which certainly still exists.

    Q88How does the kernel decide whether a sem_t from user code is valid, and why in two steps?

    First, it must be the exact start of one of SlotAllocator<_sem>'s slots, which is decided by comparing addresses and never reading memory. Then the slot's first word must be MAGIC_OPEN. Reading first could fault on a wild pointer, which panics the kernel. A magic check alone could also be fooled by a copy of a semaphore, or by the constant itself in the kernel image. The address check alone would accept a closed semaphore's free slot.

    Q89Why doesn't ~_sem clear the magic word?

    GCC 9.4 removes such a store as dead, because the object's lifetime ends right after the destructor. Instead, the kernel relies on the slot allocator writing its free-list link into the slot's first word, which is exactly where magic sits. That write cannot be removed, because the list reads it later.

    Q90Can a stale semaphore handle ever be accepted?

    Yes, once its slot has been reused by a new semaphore. Then the old handle names the new one, and a bare pointer cannot tell them apart. The FIFO slot list delays that reuse as long as possible. The PDF treats the analogous case for mem_free as undefined.

    Q91Is sem_wait_n fair?

    No. Waiters are considered in arrival order, but any waiter whose request fits is released, so a big request can be overtaken repeatedly by small ones. A newcomer whose request fits succeeds at once, as the PDF prescribes. Strict FIFO is a small change (see the drill), but it leaves threads blocked while units are free.

    Q92What do sem_wait_n(s, 0) and sem_signal_n(s, 0) do?

    wait_n(0) succeeds at once, since value >= 0 is always true. signal_n(0) adds nothing and releases nobody new.

    Q93What is the difference between a thread blocked in sem_wait and one waiting in getc?

    The first is BLOCKED: it is off the ready queue until someone signals. The second stays READY and re-tries on every turn, because a key press raises no interrupt that could wake it (chapter 10). That is also why the deadlock check never fires for a thread waiting for input.

    Q94Why does signal build a new queue instead of removing waiters in place?

    The queue is singly linked and has only put and get. Taking every waiter out and putting back those that still wait keeps their order, needs no new queue operation, and costs one pass. The final blocked = stillWaiting copies the head and tail pointers.

    Drills

    Drill 8sem_trywait: take a unit only if one is free

    Task. "Add int sem_trywait(sem_t id): if the value is positive, take one unit and return 0; otherwise return 1 immediately without blocking. Errors are negative as usual." It is the add-a-system-call pattern once more, with the work done in _sem.

    Where: the four boundary places (code 0x27, the next free one in the semaphore group); _sem::tryWait() in h/ksemaphore.hpp and src/ksemaphore.cpp; a semTryWait helper beside the other semaphore helpers in src/syscalls.cpp, using fromHandle like them.

    Watch out for: returning a negative value for "would block". It is not an error, and a caller testing < 0 would treat it as a bad handle. The 0 / 1 / negative convention used here is a common one. If the examiner specifies the return values or the code, follow them.

    The test program used: put it in test/userMain.cpp of a scratch copy of the project, in place of the public tests' userMain
    #include "../h/syscall_c.h"

namespace
{
void print(const char *text) { while (*text != '\0') { putc(*text++); } }

void show(const char *what, int result)
{
    print(what);
    if (result < 0) { putc('-'); result = -result; }
    putc((char) ('0' + result));
    putc('\n');
}
}

void userMain()
{
    sem_t s;
    sem_open(&s, 1);
    show("trywait on 1 unit:   ", sem_trywait(s));
    show("trywait on 0 units:  ", sem_trywait(s));
    sem_signal(s);
    show("after a signal:      ", sem_trywait(s));
    sem_close(s);
    show("on a closed handle:  ", sem_trywait(s));
}

    Run in the sandbox: on a semaphore opened with 1, sem_trywait returns 0, then 1. After a sem_signal it returns 0 again. On a closed handle it returns −3 (SYS_ERR_BAD_HANDLE). The own suite still passes (84 of 84).

    A C++ wrapper int Semaphore::tryWait() would be one more line. The frozen-layout rule forbids new data members, base classes and changes to the virtual functions. A new non-virtual member function changes none of those, so it should be allowed. That is a reading of the rule, not something checked with the course staff, so ask before relying on it at the defence.

    Drill 9Strict FIFO release in signal_n

    Task. "Make sem_signal_n release waiters strictly in arrival order: if the first waiter does not fit, nobody behind it may go either." Only the walk in _sem::signal changes. One flag stops the releasing at the first waiter that does not fit, and every waiter after that keeps waiting, in order.

    What does not change: wait. By the PDF's rule, a newcomer whose request fits still succeeds at once, even with others queued. Strict FIFO against newcomers would contradict "odmah uspešno", and it is worth pointing that out if this drill comes up.

    The test program used: put it in test/userMain.cpp of a scratch copy of the project, in place of the public tests' userMain
    #include "../h/syscall_c.h"

namespace
{
void print(const char *text) { while (*text != '\0') { putc(*text++); } }

sem_t s;

void wants5(void *) { sem_wait_n(s, 5); print("  T1 (wants 5) released\n"); }
void wants2(void *) { sem_wait_n(s, 2); print("  T2 (wants 2) released\n"); }

void settle() { for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { thread_dispatch(); } }
}

void userMain()
{
    sem_open(&s, 0);
    thread_t t1, t2;
    thread_create(&t1, wants5, nullptr);
    thread_create(&t2, wants2, nullptr);
    settle();                       /* T1 blocks first, then T2 */

    print("signal_n(3):\n");
    sem_signal_n(s, 3);
    settle();
    print("signal_n(2):\n");
    sem_signal_n(s, 2);
    settle();
    print("signal_n(2):\n");
    sem_signal_n(s, 2);
    settle();
    sem_close(s);
}

    Run in the sandbox with T1 (wants 5) queued before T2 (wants 2), followed by signal_n(3), signal_n(2), signal_n(2). Unmodified kernel: T2 is released by the first signal, T1 by the third. Patched kernel: nobody by the first, T1 by the second (value 5), T2 by the third. On the patched kernel exactly two own tests fail, the two that encode the original policy ("signal_n(3): T2 fits and goes, T1 keeps waiting" and the follow-up check). That is the expected change in behaviour, not a bug.

    start="10">
  • The console: getc and putc without interrupts
    • <

    Every public test for zadaci 2 and 3 prints through putc, and tests 3 and 4 read the keyboard with getc. The assignment files these calls under zadatak 4, whose intended design uses console interrupts and buffers. Without interrupts, the kernel has to wait for the UART by polling, and the design question is how to wait without stopping every other thread.

    The work is split into two layers. The device layer says whether the controller is ready and never waits. The system call decides what to do when it is not ready: give the processor away and try again later.

    h/kconsole.hpp

    h/kconsole.hpp35 lines · in the submission zip as inc/kconsole.hpp

    The k in the file name exists because the user API also has a class called Console (chapter 11). The kernel's is kernel::Console, so the two never clash, and the file names differ too.

    src/kconsole.cpp

    src/kconsole.cpp25 lines · in the submission zip as src/kconsole.cpp

    QEMU's UART is a 16550. CONSOLE_STATUS is its line status register: bit 0 means "a received byte is waiting", and bit 5 means "the transmit register is empty, you may write". CONSOLE_TX_DATA and CONSOLE_RX_DATA are the same address: a write sends a byte, a read takes the received one.

    • volatile on every access. These are device registers, not memory. Each read may return something new, and each write has an effect outside the program. Without volatile, the compiler could keep the status in a register and never see the bit change.
    • The addresses are read where they are used. CONSOLE_STATUS is an extern const defined in hw.lib, so its value is not known when this file is compiled. A global such as volatile uint8 *status = (volatile uint8 *) CONSOLE_STATUS; would need a dynamic initialiser, and this kernel never runs any, so the pointer would silently stay null.

    The waiting policy, in the dispatcher

    If the controller is not ready, the thread calls _thread::dispatch() and gives the processor to the next ready thread, exactly as THREAD_DISPATCH does. It goes to the back of the ready queue as READY and tries again when its turn comes back. This works because kernel code runs on the thread's own stack (chapter 1, decision 1): a thread can be switched away in the middle of a system call and continue inside it later.

    The dispatcher cases that use these helpers are in chapter 7 (syscalls.cpp:176–185). GETC returns the byte zero-extended ((uint8)), and PUTC returns SYS_OK.

    Why not spin, and why not block? Spinning (while (!tryGet(c)) {}) inside the kernel would freeze the whole system, because nothing preempts a thread in this kernel. Every other thread, including the producers in tests 3 and 4, would stop until a key arrived. Blocking in the semaphore sense (off the ready queue until someone wakes you) would need someone to do the waking. That is normally the console interrupt, and this kernel enables none, so a blocked reader would never wake. Re-trying while READY is the one option that works without interrupts. It also means waiting for input is never reported as a deadlock: a waiting reader is always in the ready queue.

    Why not console.lib? The faculty's __getc waits by spinning, without yielding, until hw.lib's console interrupt handler has put a character into its buffer. In a cooperative kernel that would freeze every thread between keystrokes, even with interrupts on, and tests 3 and 4 need the producers to keep running while one thread waits for the keyboard. In this kernel, which enables no interrupts and never calls console_handler, it would not return at all (the independent review found this in console.lib's disassembly). Dropping console.lib from LIBS is one of the two Makefile changes the assignment permits.

    This used to be in the C API. Until Phase 6, GETC and PUTC tried once and returned, and the C API functions looped, calling thread_dispatch() between attempts. That worked, but it broke the rule that every ABI call has the C API's semantics, except mem_alloc and thread_create: a program issuing the raw GETC would not wait. The PDF calls that option "jednostavnije, ali manje robusno". Moving the loop into the kernel cost a few lines and removed the deviation. Aleksandar decided the move. The own tests check that the raw ABI call waits: a helper thread feeds a key through the UART's loopback mode while the main test thread sits in a raw GETC.

    A keystroke can be lost if the UART's receive FIFO (16 bytes on a 16550) fills before any thread polls it. That needs typing faster than the ready queue goes round, and in tests 3 and 4 the typed letters did arrive in order and none was lost, both sent at once and typed one every 0.3 seconds. The robust fix is interrupt-driven input into a ring buffer, which is zadatak 4 material.

    Questions

    Q95How does getc wait for a key without stopping the other threads?

    Inside the kernel, GETC loops on Console::tryGet. Each time the UART has nothing, it calls _thread::dispatch(): the thread goes to the back of the ready queue and the others run. When its turn comes back, it tries again. The thread is READY the whole time.

    Q96Why is a thread waiting for input READY and not BLOCKED?

    A BLOCKED thread needs someone to unblock it. For the console that would be the interrupt handler when a byte arrives, and this kernel enables no interrupts. So it must keep re-trying, which means staying in the ready queue.

    Q97Why did you not use console.lib?

    Its __getc spins without yielding until the console interrupt handler delivers a character. In a kernel without preemption that stops every thread until a key is pressed, and public tests 3 and 4 need the producer threads to run meanwhile. With no interrupts enabled, as here, it would never return at all. The Makefile may be changed only to drop mem.lib and console.lib from LIBS, and that is what was done.

    Q98Why is the waiting loop in the kernel and not in the C API?

    The ABI section says every ABI call has the same semantics as its C API function, except mem_alloc and thread_create. So a raw GETC must wait just like getc(). With the loop in the C API, the raw call would return at once.

    Q99Why does kernel::Console read CONSOLE_STATUS every time instead of keeping a pointer in a global?

    CONSOLE_STATUS is defined in hw.lib, so its value is not a compile-time constant here. A global initialised from it would need a dynamic initialiser, which nothing runs in this kernel. The global would silently stay 0.

    Q100How would the console work with interrupts, as zadatak 4 intends?

    Enable SEIE, and on an external interrupt ask the PLIC which device raised it (plic_claim), handle it, and acknowledge it (plic_complete). Input: the handler moves received bytes into a kernel ring buffer and signals a semaphore that getc waits on, so a reader could then truly block. Output: putc puts bytes into an output buffer, and a kernel thread or the handler feeds the UART when it reports it can take more. The system call layer would stay the same.

    start="11">
  • The C++ API
    • <

    The C++ layer runs in user mode and uses nothing but the C API. Almost every member function is one C API call. The interesting parts are the few rules the assignment adds on top: a thread object can run either a function or its own run(); a destructor may have to release or synchronise; and the class layouts may not change at all.

    The class definitions in syscall_cpp.hpp are given, and their layout must not change: no new non-static data members, no new base classes, no change to the set or order of virtual functions, no changed signatures, because precompiled user code relies on the layout. Thread(body, arg) creates a thread object that is started with start(). If a derived class overrides run() and was also constructed with a function pointer, the function pointer wins. new and delete go through mem_alloc and mem_free. "Zadatak je u potpunosti implementirati sve ove klase i operacije": every class, PeriodicThread included.

    h/syscall_cpp.hpp

    h/syscall_cpp.hpp95 lines · in the submission zip as inc/syscall_cpp.hpp

    The array forms, new[] and delete[], are not in the assignment's listing. They are free functions, so they add nothing to any class layout. Without them, the first new T[n] anywhere would be a link error, because there is no C++ runtime library to supply them.

    The three data members and the two virtual functions are exactly the assignment's. The one addition, runWrapper, is a static member function. Static members are not stored in objects, so the layout, sizeof(Thread) and the virtual table are unchanged.

    PeriodicThread gets the same treatment: periodicBody is a private static member, so the frozen layout is untouched.

    src/syscall_cpp.cpp

    src/syscall_cpp.cpp162 lines · in the submission zip as src/syscall_cpp.cpp

    new and delete

    new on an exhausted heap. The frozen header declares the global operator new without noexcept, and standard C++ does not allow adding it: the language implicitly declares this function as one that may throw, and a replacement must match. (GCC 9.4 happens to accept a noexcept version when <new> is not included, but that is a compiler quirk, not something to rely on.) So the compiler assumes it never returns nullptr and runs the constructor on whatever comes back. If mem_alloc fails, that is address 0. The constructor's first store faults in user mode, and the fault path ends that thread (chapter 6). Without exceptions there is no standard way to report the failure. The kernel's own classes avoid the problem with a noexcept class-specific operator new (chapter 4).

    Thread

    The two constructors are where "the function pointer always wins" is settled, once. Thread(body, arg) stores what it is given. The protected Thread(), used by classes that override run(), stores body = &Thread::runWrapper and arg = this. start() always runs body(arg). So run() is reached only for objects made with Thread(). An object made with a function pointer never calls run(), whatever it overrides.

    The kernel frees a thread's control block and stack by itself, at the dispatch after the thread finishes. So there is nothing for the destructor to give back. The handle may already name a freed slot, so it is not touched. The object must outlive its thread. If it is deleted while its thread still runs, runWrapper's object becomes a dangling pointer. The public tests delete their Thread objects only after the threads have signalled that they are finished.

    • start() refuses a second start with SYS_ERR_GENERIC. myHandle is written by the kernel only when thread_create succeeds, so after a failed start the object can try again.
    • runWrapper turns the void * back into a Thread * and makes a virtual call, so it reaches the most derived run(). The virtual table pointer is the derived class's by the time the new thread runs. start() puts the new thread at the back of the ready queue, and it cannot run until its creator gives up the processor. So even a start() called inside a constructor is safe in this kernel, as long as the object is fully constructed before the creator's next dispatch.
    • sleep is time_sleep, which answers SYS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED in this kernel.

    Semaphore

    If sem_open fails, myHandle stays nullptr, and every later wait() or signal() gets SYS_ERR_BAD_HANDLE from the kernel. Nothing crashes, and the failure is visible to the caller. The destructor closes the semaphore, which releases any thread still inside wait() with SYS_ERR_SEM_CLOSED. That is safe: wait() reads myHandle before the system call and touches nothing in the object after it returns, so deleting a Semaphore while threads wait on it leaves them nothing freed to read.

    PeriodicThread

    A periodic thread is an ordinary Thread whose body is periodicBody, passed through the function-pointer constructor. By the rule above, run() plays no part: periodicActivation() is what a derived class redefines.

    terminate() has to stop the loop, but the frozen class has no room for a flag: period is its only data member. So the request travels in period itself. 0 means "terminated", and a thread created with period 0 ends without activating at all. The thread finishes after the activation in progress.

    Without a timer, time_sleep always fails, so the loop calls thread_dispatch() instead. Activations then come once per round of the ready queue rather than once per period. With a working time_sleep (zadatak 4) the same loop would be truly periodic, and nothing in this class would change.

    period is not volatile, and it does not need to be. Every pass of the loop calls functions the compiler cannot see into (a virtual function, time_sleep, thread_dispatch). Any of them could change thread->period, so the compiler must read it again each time round. With no preemption, terminate() from another thread can only run while this thread is inside one of those calls.

    Console

    ::getc and ::putc name the global C API functions. Without the ::, getc() inside the class would find the static member Console::getc first and call itself for ever.

    Questions

    Q101How does a class that overrides run() get its run() executed on a new thread?

    It is constructed through the protected Thread(), which sets body = &Thread::runWrapper and arg = this. start() creates a kernel thread over body(arg). In the new thread, runWrapper(this) casts back to Thread * and calls run(), a virtual call that reaches the derived class's override.

    Q102A derived class overrides run() and also passes a function to Thread(body, arg). Which one runs?

    The function. The assignment says so, and the code makes it automatic: only the protected constructor ever sets the body to runWrapper, the only path that calls run().

    Q103Why is runWrapper a static member function?

    The kernel needs a plain void (*)(void *) for the thread body, and a non-static member function cannot be one. Being static also means it adds nothing to the object, so the frozen layout is unchanged. Being private keeps it out of the public interface.

    Q104What happens if start() is called twice?

    The second call sees myHandle != nullptr and returns SYS_ERR_GENERIC without creating anything.

    Q105Why does ~Thread() do nothing? What if a Thread is deleted while its thread still runs?

    The kernel frees the thread's control block and stack itself when the thread finishes, and the handle may already be stale, so there is nothing safe to do. Deleting the object while its thread runs is the caller's mistake: runWrapper's pointer to the object would dangle. The object must outlive its thread.

    Q106What does new do when the heap is exhausted?

    mem_alloc returns nullptr, and operator new passes it on. The given header declares the global operator new without noexcept, as the standard requires, so the compiler does not check for null and runs the constructor at address 0. That store faults in user mode and ends the thread. There is no exception mechanism to do better.

    Q107What happens to threads blocked in Semaphore::wait() when the Semaphore object is deleted?

    ~Semaphore calls sem_close, which releases them, and their wait() returns SYS_ERR_SEM_CLOSED. wait() does not touch the deleted object after the system call returns, so this is safe.

    Q108How does PeriodicThread::terminate() work when the class may not get a new data member?

    It sets period to 0, which the loop in periodicBody reads as "stop" on its next test. The thread ends after its current activation.

    Q109Did you change the frozen class layouts?

    No. Two private static member functions were added: Thread::runWrapper and PeriodicThread::periodicBody. Static members are not part of an object's layout, the virtual functions are untouched, and every given signature is unchanged. The array new[] and delete[] are free functions.

    Q110Why does Console::getc call ::getc and not getc?

    Inside the class, the unqualified name getc means the member function itself, so the call would recurse for ever. ::getc names the C API function in the global namespace.

    start="12">
  • End-to-end traces
    • <

    Each trace follows one event through every layer, with a link to the exact lines at each step. They are the best preparation for "walk me through what happens when…" questions. If you can narrate each trace without the links, you know the kernel.

    Trace 1: from main() to the first user instruction

    1. hw.lib's start-up code (system_main → userinit) calls main() in supervisor mode, on stack0 (main.cpp:15–20).
    2. System::initialize masks every interrupt source in sie (system.cpp:37), builds the heap's free list (system.cpp:39), points stvec at trapEntry (system.cpp:40), and wraps the running code in the main thread (system.cpp:41, tcb.cpp:68–74).
    3. System::run takes a 64-block stack from the allocator (system.cpp:52–54) and calls _thread::create for userMainBody (system.cpp:58).
    4. create checks its arguments (tcb.cpp:83–85), takes a slot with new (tcb.cpp:87), and the constructor fabricates a YieldFrame at the top of the stack: ra = threadStart, s1 = userMainBody, s2 = nullptr (tcb.cpp:38–48). The thread joins the ready queue (tcb.cpp:92).
    5. Back in run, one user thread is alive and the queue is not empty, so the main thread calls _thread::dispatch() (system.cpp:82).
    6. dispatch makes the main thread READY and queues it behind userMain's thread (tcb.cpp:113–117), takes userMain's thread from the front (tcb.cpp:124), and calls yield(&main->sp, &userMain->sp) (tcb.cpp:128).
    7. yield pushes the main thread's ra and s0–s11 on stack0, stores sp, loads the new thread's sp, pops the fabricated frame, and ret jumps to threadStart (asm_routines.cpp:126–158).
    8. threadStart moves s1, s2 into a0, a1, sets sepc = threadWrapper, clears SPP, and executes sret (asm_routines.cpp:174–180).
    9. In user mode: threadWrapper(userMainBody, nullptr) calls userMainBody, which calls userMain() (syscall_c.cpp:68–72, system.cpp:20–23), and the test menu appears.

    Trace 2: thread_dispatch() from thread A to thread B

    Both threads have run before, and B is at the head of the ready queue.

    1. A calls thread_dispatch(), which calls __syscall(0x13, 0, 0, 0, 0) (syscall_c.cpp:58–61), which executes ecall (asm_routines.cpp:18).
    2. Hardware: sepc ← the ecall's address, SPP ← 0, scause ← 8, jump to trapEntry.
    3. trapEntry pushes a 256-byte frame onto A's stack and saves every register, sepc and sstatus (asm_routines.cpp:32–68), then calls trapHandler(frame) (asm_routines.cpp:70–71).
    4. trapHandler: not an interrupt. It is ecall from user mode, so frame->sepc += 4 and Syscalls::dispatch runs (trap.cpp:90–95).
    5. case THREAD_DISPATCH calls _thread::dispatch() (syscalls.cpp:134–139).
    6. dispatch: A is RUNNING, so it becomes READY at the back of the queue. B is taken from the front, and yield(&A->sp, &B->sp) runs (tcb.cpp:112–128).
    7. yield pushes A's YieldFrame on A's stack, saves A's sp, loads B's, pops B's YieldFrame, and ret jumps into B's own earlier yield() call (asm_routines.cpp:126–158).
    8. B's dispatch() returns. B finishes whatever system call it was in (if it was also a THREAD_DISPATCH: frame.a0 = SYS_OK), trapHandler returns, and B's trapEntry epilogue reloads B's sstatus and sepc from B's frame, restores B's registers, and executes sret (asm_routines.cpp:73–110). B continues in user mode.
    9. When some later dispatch picks A, the mirror image happens: A's yield returns, A's frame.a0 = SYS_OK, A's epilogue restores A's registers, including the t1 that public test 1 checks, and A continues after its ecall.

    Trace 3: thread_create until the new thread's first instruction

    1. thread_create(&h, f, arg) refuses a null &h, then allocates the stack with mem_alloc(4096): a first system call, MEM_ALLOC with 64 blocks (syscall_c.cpp:34–44).
    2. __syscall(THREAD_CREATE, &h, f, arg, stack + 4096) makes a second trap (syscall_c.cpp:46–48).
    3. In the kernel, threadCreate checks that &h is an aligned address in RAM (syscalls.cpp:42–48). _thread::create refuses a null body or a stack that is not a live 4096-byte block, then builds the thread with its fabricated first frame, writes h, counts the thread, and queues it (tcb.cpp:76–94).
    4. SYS_OK goes back through frame.a0. The creator continues. If the kernel had refused, the C API would free the stack (syscall_c.cpp:49).
    5. When a later dispatch() reaches the new thread, yield "returns" into threadStart, which executes sret into threadWrapper(f, arg) in user mode, which calls f(arg). Steps 7–9 of trace 1 apply unchanged.

    Trace 4: sem_wait blocks, sem_signal releases

    Semaphore s has value 0. Thread T1 waits, thread T2 signals.

    1. T1: sem_wait(s) makes a trap with SEM_WAIT. semWait vets the handle with _sem::fromHandle (syscalls.cpp:69–75, ksemaphore.cpp:56–68).
